CMP00.001/ Homage to the illustrious Vajrasattva. CMP00.002/ Pay homage to that which is equal to space, devoid of intrinsic nature, and pure; pay homage to that which is entirely without syllables and inexpressible. Chapter One: The Section on Awakening, Reunion, and the Resolution of Doubts.

CMP01.001: Here, in this Vajrayāna, for the sake of those teachers who practice the oral transmission of the two types of mantra, who are devoted to mantra, devoted to the inner science (adhyātma), and who have mastered the scriptures; and for the sake of those who desire to benefit all sentient beings by clarifying the meaning and words spoken in the sūtras, these illuminating manuals on the branches of sādhana are composed, extracted from the *Sadbhāva-tantra*, through compositions of secret terminology consisting of various arrangements of verses, gāthās, āryās, and other poetic forms, adorned with many graceful and elegant words and phrases, for the purpose of awakening the ignorant.

CMP01.002: This was appropriate for the Kṛta, Tretā, and Dvāpara ages, when people were endowed with longevity, health, prosperity, and virtues such as generosity and ethical conduct; being devoted to the pursuit of the scriptures, they were intent upon the knowledge of reality, and thus the reality was communicated to them through subtle words and elegant phrasing, and they understood it.

CMP01.003. Now, however, in the Kali age, people are deprived of long life, health, and prosperity; their minds are characterized by deceit, hypocrisy, wickedness, pride, envy, and malice; they are deficient in wisdom and hold false views. Devoted to evil deeds, they are unable to determine the meanings of words hidden within the *Lalitavistara* and other such texts, and thus they do not seek the ultimate reality (*tattva*). Consequently, failing to realize the truth due to the distraction of studying non-Buddhist treatises, they pass away and remain devoted solely to their auspicious and inauspicious karma.
Therefore, for those desiring liberation, resorting to the medium of speech such as playful expressions, eroticism, and so forth, is useless, because words are like a raft;
as it was said by the Blessed One: "One should rely on the meaning, but the word may be this way or that."

CMP01.004/ Having understood this essential point and having attained the samādhi of the completion stage (*niṣpannakrama*) through the sequence of the generation stage (*utpattikrama*) according to the tradition of the venerable Nāgārjuna, I shall explain the *Sūtramelāpaka* for the sake of clarifying the five stages, as a common teaching for both refined and unrefined disciples by means of clear terminology. This includes the reality of mantra (*mantratattva*), the reality of the seal (*mudrātattva*), the reality of the self (*ātmatattva*), and the reality of the deity (*devatātattva*). CMP01.005/ "Those devoid of reality do not achieve accomplishment even in hundreds of millions of aeons," so it was said by the Blessed One throughout all the recitations of his teachings, such as the *Sūtrakā* and others.
As it was said by the Blessed One in the *Caturdevīparipṛcchā-mahāyogatantra*:
"Among the eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dharma of the Great Sage,
all those who do not know the reality (tattva) are indeed fruitless."
CMP01.008: The Vajra-disciple said:

"The Blessed One has stated that without the knowledge of reality (*tattva-jñāna*), Buddhahood cannot be attained; therefore, I wish to hear the definition of reality by way of the scriptural teachings, since the Mahāyāna dialecticians and others, relying on the provisional meaning (*neyārtha*), conceptualize reality in various ways."
For the sake of gathering them together, may the Blessed One speak: what is this that is called reality?
The Vajra Guru said:
That which is as it truly is—that is reality.
CMP01.010: He asked: "Bhagavān, what is this that is called 'reality' (bhūta)? CMP01.011: He replied:
"That which is non-deceptive is the real.
[The interlocutor] asks: "What is this so-called 'non-deceptiveness'?"
He said:
"That meditative absorption which consists of the method of reality is non-deceptive.
He said: [CMP01.014]
"What is this so-called 'samādhi whose nature is the ultimate reality'?
He replied:
"That which is characterized by the non-duality of the two truths is the samādhi whose nature is the ultimate reality."
CMP01.016: He asked, "Bhagavān, what is this that is called the two truths?
CMP01.017: He replied:
The first is conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) and the second is ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya).
He asked: "Blessed One, what are the characteristics of these two truths?"
The Vajra Master said:
"It was taught by the Blessed One in the *Vajroṣṇīṣa-tantra*.
Vajrapāṇi said:
“Blessed One, how is it that the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is the *ālaya* of all phenomena?
The Blessed One replied:

“O Lord of Secrets, all phenomena consist of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*), including the world of the moving and the stationary; for they have the ultimate truth as their support by way of being non-abiding (*asthāna-yogena*).”
Ultimate truth is selfless, unconquered, entirely empty, without increase or decrease, utterly pure, equal to space, stainless by nature, syllable-less, ineffable, devoid of body, speech, and mind;
it neither exists nor does not exist, and it neither moves nor does not move.
It is neither distant nor near, neither empty nor non-empty, and it is not even a middle;
this is the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).
Therefore, for that which is supremely profound and difficult to fathom, characterized by non-arising and non-ceasing, there is the conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*) as its condition.

First, conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) is like a dream, a magical illusion, or a reflection in a mirror; it is the meditative absorption of illusion (*māyā-samādhi*), its own characteristic, and the cause of the four divine abodes (*brahma-vihāra*).
Through these two, there is the process of simultaneous integration (*yuganaddha-vāhi-krama*).
This very samādhi, which consists of the method of reality,
is the cessation of all apprehension;
this is the entirety of reality.
The Vajra-disciple said:

"Ordinary persons like us, through our attachment to the various external phenomena that have existed since beginningless time, are fixated on the conceptualizations and habitual tendencies regarding intrinsic nature—namely, non-existence, existence, unity, multiplicity, both, neither, 'neither exists nor does not exist,' and permanence or impermanence. When training in the meditative absorption of the completion stage (*niṣpannakrama-samādhi*), do they train according to a gradual sequence, or rather, does it manifest instantaneously for them by means of the guru’s instruction alone?"
CMP01.023/ The Vajraguru said:
"They train by way of gradual progression, not simultaneously"—this was indeed taught by the Blessed One in the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*.
CMP01.024/ Then, Mahāmati the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva again requested the Blessed One for the sake of purifying the stream of appearances of his own mind.
“Blessed One, how is the stream of what is seen as one’s own mind purified— simultaneously or gradually?
The Blessed One replied,
“Mahāmati, the stream of what is seen as one’s own mind is purified gradually.”
They do not ripen simultaneously, Mahāmati; for example, mango fruits ripen gradually and not all at once.
In the same way, Mahāmati, the Tathāgata gradually purifies the stream of what is seen by the minds of all sentient beings, not all at once;
just as, Mahāmati, a potter makes his vessels gradually.
In the same way, Mahāmati, the Tathāgata purifies the stream of what is seen as one's own mind for all sentient beings gradually,
not simultaneously.
CMP01.027: For example, Mahāmati, just as all the grasses, shrubs, herbs, and trees on the earth grow gradually and not all at once,
even so, Mahāmati, the Tathāgata gradually purifies the stream of what is seen as one's own mind for all sentient beings.
Not simultaneously,
Mahāmati; just as, for example, laughter, dance, song, painting, lute-playing, and drawing proceed sequentially and not all at once.
In the same way, Mahāmati, the Tathāgata gradually purifies the stream of what is seen by the minds of all sentient beings,
not all at once.
Demonstrating this very sequence clearly in the Śūraṅgama-sūtra, he said:
CMP01.030. Then, the bodhisattva mahāsattva Dṛḍhamati said this to the Blessed One:
"Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, training in what way, train in this Śūraṅgama samādhi by means of the non-conceit regarding all training?"
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the bodhisattva Dṛḍhamati: "It is just as if, Dṛḍhamati,
a pupil of a master archer were first to pierce a cow-hair target."
When he has been trained on a cow-hide target, then he pierces a wooden board;
when he has been trained on a wooden board, then he pierces a mark;
when he has been trained on a mark, then he pierces a staff.
When he has been trained with a staff, then he pierces a hundred-hair target; when he has been trained with a hundred-hair target, then he pierces a ten-hair target;
when he has been trained with a ten-hair target, then he pierces a single hair.
When he has been trained in the basics, he then pierces at sound;
when he has been trained in piercing at sound, he then pierces without missing;
when he has been trained in piercing without missing, he then becomes proficient in the training of archery.
Desiring this, in the darkness of the night, whatever sound he hears—whether of a human or a non-human—he goes effortlessly toward that very source as if it were a straight arrow.
Established in the piercing of sound, he does not train anywhere;
for what reason?
O Dṛḍhamati, because he was well-trained previously, those previous impulses manifest themselves to him in this very way.
For a bodhisattva established in this Śūraṅgama Samādhi, there is no longer anything further to be learned regarding any dharma.
Why is that?
Because, through having been well-trained in the past, all the qualities and dharmas of a bodhisattva become manifest through this very samādhi.
CMP01.033: By this method, one who wishes to train in the Śūraṅgama-samādhi by relying on the Vajrayāna should train according to this sequence;
therein, this is the sequence:
first, one trains in the aspiration for the Buddha-vehicle.
When one has trained in the aspiration for the Buddha-vehicle, then one trains in the single-minded concentration of the nine vehicles;
when one has trained in the nine vehicles, then one trains in the yoga of the imagined;
when one becomes established in the concentration of a beginner, then one enters into the hundredfold differentiation of lineages.
When one understands the isolation of the body (*kāya-viveka*) through the lineage of the hundred families, then one becomes established in the *samādhi* of the Body-Vajra.
Having remained in the isolation of the body, one enters the isolation of speech (*vāk-viveka*) by way of the gateway of *āli* and *kāli*.
When one has attained the regulation of breath (*prāṇāyāma*) through the sequence of Vajra-recitation (*vajra-jāpa*), then one becomes established in the *samādhi* of the Speech-Vajra.
Abiding in the discernment of speech, one enters the discernment of the mind through the sequence of the manifestation of primordial nature (*prakṛti*).
When one trains in the manifestation of primordial nature as it truly is—the various movements driven by the winds—one becomes absorbed in the *samādhi* of the Mind-Vajra.
Abiding in the thorough knowledge of the mind as it truly is, one enters into conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) by means of the twelve similes of illusion.
When one has entered the illusion-like samādhi, then one receives the empowerment of all Buddhas;
abiding in the illusion-like samādhi, one enters the ultimate truth by means of the sequence of the eighteen great emptinesses.
When one enters the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) through the samādhi that breaks down the grasping at a composite whole, then one becomes purified of all afflictions.

When, having emerged through the sequence of knowledge (*jñānakrama*), one awakens to oneself as naturally luminous by means of the non-duality of the two truths, then one has become trained in the meditative absorption of the completion stage (*niṣpannakrama*).
Having entered the meditative absorption of the completion stage, the great yogin no longer trains in any phenomenon whatsoever, because he has already been well-trained;
just as an archery master who stands at the point of hitting a sound does not train in anything further.
Why? Because, due to having been well-trained previously,
it manifests through the power of that prior momentum (*pūrvāvedha*).

In the same way, one who is established in the meditative absorption of the completion stage (*niṣpannakrama*) becomes one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) because of having been well-trained previously; thus,
his mundane and supramundane accomplishments (*siddhi*) manifest spontaneously, without effort.
CMP01.036: Thus, one training in the samādhi of the completion stage trains by way of successive stages, not simultaneously;
therefore, without physical isolation (*kāya-viveka*), vocal isolation (*vāk-viveka*) cannot be understood.
The realization of mental isolation cannot be achieved by one who lacks verbal isolation;
conventional truth cannot be directly realized without the realization of the manifestation of primordial nature;
and ultimate truth cannot be directly realized without the realization of conventional truth.
Without the realization of ultimate truth, it is impossible to directly manifest the stage of simultaneous progression (*yuganaddha-vāhi-krama*).
Knowing this essential point, the Blessed One said:
"One trains by means of gradual progression."

"Not simultaneously" means that when the sequential process has been mastered through gradual practice, it is taught by the Blessed One himself in the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* (CMP 01.038) that the stream of what is perceived by one's own mind becomes purified simultaneously.
For example, Mahāmati, all appearances of forms within a mirror are seen simultaneously and without conceptual construction.

In the same way, Mahāmati, the Tathāgata simultaneously purifies for all sentient beings the stream of what is seen as their own mind, making it free from conceptual construction and within the range of the non-manifest.
Just as, Mahāmati, the orbs of the moon and the sun simultaneously illuminate all forms with their rays, so it is said:
[The Buddha] said this:
CMP01.041/ This is the means devised by the Perfect Buddhas for leading beginner beings to enter the ultimate truth; CMP01.042/ like a staircase, it has been constructed.
CMP01.043/ Without the five successive stages, the meditative absorption of the completion stage cannot be attained.

CMP02.001: The Vajra-disciple said:
"O Blessed One, how should one first train in the isolation of one's own body?"
The Vajra Master said:
"Excellent, excellent, O Great Being! I shall explain to you in detail the seclusion of the body.
In that regard, four elements bring about the formation of the body."
Once the body has been fully formed, its constituent parts are set aside in heaps:
namely, the muscles of flesh, sinews, veins, arteries, brain, bones, marrow, intestines, mesentery, kidneys, heart, and stomach.

It is a collection and an aggregate consisting of the lungs, liver, urine, feces, the stomach, the intestines, fat, lymph, pus, blood, bile, phlegm, snot, hair of the head, beard, nails, body hair, skin, hands, feet, eyes, limbs, and so forth.
CMP02.003. Furthermore, in that context, the five aggregates, the four elements, the six sense bases, the five objects, and the five cognitions are called a "heap" (*rāśi*).
Just as collections of grain, barley, sesame, wheat, and mung beans are called heaps, in the same way, the collection of the major and minor limbs contained within the body is called a heap.

In the conjunction of the elements (*dhātu-samavāya*), the continuity of ignorance, latent tendencies, craving, and afflictions— consisting of wisdom, views, mind, and so forth— is called an accumulation (*sañcaya*). However, no accumulation or heap of consciousness (*vijñāna*) is perceived,
because it is without a substratum (*anālayatva*).
As it is said in the *Bhadrapāliparipṛcchā*:
"In this body, consciousness is not established anywhere,
nor is a body perceived apart from consciousness."
"Therefore, Bhadrapāla, one who has not yet seen the Truths does not perceive this consciousness,
nor does its vision become as clear as a myrobalan fruit in the palm of the hand.

Furthermore, the nature of these aggregates, elements, and sense-fields— which have been established through beginningless, innate egoism— is now described as being composed of the atoms of all the Tathāgatas."
CMP02.006. In brief, the five aggregates are proclaimed as the five Buddhas.
CMP02.007. The vajra-sense bases themselves are the supreme maṇḍala of the Bodhisattvas.
CMP02.008. Earth is known as Locanā; the water element is remembered as Māmakī.
Fire is known as Pāṇḍarā, and wind is proclaimed as Tārā.
The mantra practitioner should always meditate upon the deity through forms, sounds, and so forth.
Thus it was spoken by the Blessed One in the *Śrī-Guhyasamāja-Mahāyoga-Tantra*.
CMP02.012/ Furthermore, these aggregates, elements, and so forth, when each divided into five aspects, become one hundred.
CMP02.013/ The families are said to be of one hundred kinds, but in brief they are fivefold.
CMP02.014/ They further attain a threefold state through the application of body, speech, and mind.
CMP02.015/ According to the statement in the *Śrīguhyendutilaka*,
we shall first demonstrate the division into one hundred families.
CMP02.016/ Among those, the aggregate of the form-skandha is Vairocana.
Furthermore, when divided into five aspects, it is empowered by the five Tathāgatas:

therein, the form of external, internal, and both [external and internal] configurations—such as long, short, and so forth—is the empowerment of Vairocana; the form of both types [of self-grasping], such as the conceit of a self (*ātma-manyanā*) and so forth, is that of Ratnasambhava.
The form consisting of the five colors, such as blue and so forth, both externally and internally, is the empowerment of Amitābha;
the form appearing as the light of the moon and sun, both externally and internally, is that of Amoghasiddhi;
and the form of representation (*vijñapti*) which is merely self-cognizable is that of Akṣobhya.
The aggregate of form has been explained in five ways.
With reference to the Ratnasambhava samādhi, it is said:
the collection of the aggregate of feeling is Ratnasambhava.
Furthermore, she is empowered by the five Tathāgatas:
therein, the sensation arising from bile in the gathering [of humors] belongs to Akṣobhya,
and the sensation born of phlegm and wind belongs to Ratnasambhava.
Pleasant feeling is the empowerment of Amitābha, painful feeling is that of Amoghasiddhi,
and neutral feeling is that of Vairocana; thus the aggregate of feeling is said to be fivefold.
CMP02.018: With reference to the *Amitābha-samādhi*, it is said that Amitābha is the aggregate of the mass of perceptions (*saṃjñā-skandha*).

Although the stationary and moving entities produced here are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), they possess distinct perceptions because they are differentiated by categories such as footless, two-footed, and so forth; having grasped those [perceptions] through consciousness (*vijñāna*), a discernment is made.
That sign is established separately as the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*).
Furthermore, that perception is empowered by the five Tathāgatas;
therein, the perception of "two-footed beings" belongs to Akṣobhya.
The perception of four-footed beings belongs to Ratnasambhava; the perception of footless beings belongs to Amitābha; the perception of many-footed beings belongs to Amoghasiddhi.
"The designations 'immobile' and 'stationary' are the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of Vairocana"— thus has the aggregate of perception (*sañjñā-skandha*) been explained in its fivefold aspect.
Now, with reference to the *Amoghasiddhi* samādhi, he says:
The aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is Amoghasiddhi;
furthermore, he is empowered by the five Tathāgatas.
Among those, the formation of body (*kāya-saṃskāra*) belongs to Vairocana.
The refinement of speech belongs to Amitābha;
the refinement of mind belongs to Akṣobhya;
the refinement of the earth, atmosphere, and heaven belongs to Ratnasambhava.
The consecration of liberation is said to be the empowerment of Amoghasiddhi; thus, the aggregate of consecrations is fivefold.
With reference to the samādhi of Akṣobhya, he says:
That apprehension of an object which determines the object— that realization of the object— is consciousness (*vijñāna*);
and by means of the aspect (*ākāra*) mounted upon that consciousness, the external object is designated.
Consciousness is designated by means of an external object;
thus, the establishment of both the knower and the known occurs through mutual dependence.
Furthermore, that consciousness, when divided fivefold, is presided over by the five Tathāgatas.
In that regard, the aggregate of consciousness is Akṣobhya;
visual consciousness belongs to Vairocana,
and auditory consciousness belongs to Ratnasambhava.
Olfactory consciousness is the empowerment of Amitābha; gustatory consciousness is that of Amoghasiddhi; and tactile consciousness is that of Akṣobhya.
The aggregate of consciousness has been explained in five ways. In brief, the five aggregates are proclaimed to be the five Buddhas;
such is the meaning of this sūtra.
CMP02.023: With reference to the four elements, it is said:
therein, what is the earth element? It is that which is heaviness and solidity, and its function is supporting.
In that regard, what is the water element?
It is that which is fluidity, moisture, and has the function of cohesion.
In that regard, what is the fire element?
Regarding that which has the nature of heat, ripening, and the function of drying—
among these, what is the wind element? That which consists of contraction, extension, inhalation, exhalation, and light movement— that is the wind element.

CMP02.024: Thus, having established the specific characteristics of the four elements according to the sequence of the Mahāyāna, now, for the purpose of removing ordinary ego-clinging, one is made to consist of the five Buddhas according to the sequence of the Vajrayāna.
In that regard, the aggregate of the earth element is Locanā.
Furthermore, being divided into five aspects, it is empowered by the five Tathāgatas as follows:
hair, bone, feces, spleen, and heart belong to Vairocana; while body hair, nails, pus, and heart belong to Ratnasambhava.
The teeth, skin, flesh, and heart are the empowerment of Amitābha;
the sinews, flesh, ribs, and heart are the empowerment of Amoghasiddhi;
and the impurities, intestines, bile, and heart are the empowerment of Akṣobhya.
As it is said in the *Vajramālā*:
"Relying upon the five hearts, it emerges from the five threads;
joined with the five winds, it effects the enjoyment of the five desires."
CMP02.028: Furthermore, in this way, the external earth element is also divided into five aspects:
the four continents and Sumeru.
Among these, Sumeru is the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of Mahāvairocana.
Pūrvavideha is the domain of Akṣobhya; Jambūdvīpa is the domain of Ratnasambhava; Aparagodānīya is the domain of Amitābha.
It is said that Uttarakuru is the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of Amoghasiddhi; thus the earth element is fivefold.
With reference to the *māmakī*-samādhi, it says:
Therein, the collection of the water element is Māmakī;
furthermore, it is empowered by the five Tathāgatas,
wherein the phlegm and the tears are the empowerment of Vairocana.
Urine is the empowerment of Akṣobhya;
sweat is the empowerment of Ratnasambhava;
blood is the empowerment of Amitābha.
Saliva is the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of Amoghasiddhi (CMP 02.030).
Furthermore, even externally it is seen in five forms;
therein, the water of the ocean belongs to Akṣobhya.
River water belongs to Ratnasambhava;
spring water belongs to Amitābha;
and pond water belongs to Amoghasiddhi.
"The water of the mountain torrent is the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of Vairocana"—
thus the water element is said to be fivefold.
With reference to the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) of Pāṇḍaravāsinī, he says:
The aggregate of the fire element is Pāṇḍaravāsinī;
furthermore, she is empowered by the five Tathāgatas,
and the heat of the head is the empowerment of Vairocana.
The heat of the heart belongs to Akṣobhya; the heat of the navel belongs to Ratnasambhava;
the heat of all limbs belongs to Amitābha.
"The belly is the hot [element], the empowerment of Amoghasiddhi" (CMP 02.032).
Furthermore, even externally it is seen in five aspects;
therein, the *āhavanīya* fire belongs to Akṣobhya.
Fire produced from stone belongs to Vairocana;
fire produced from sun-crystals belongs to Ratnasambhava;
and fire produced from wood belongs to Amitābha.
"The forest fire is said to be the empowerment (adhiṣṭhāna) of Amoghasiddhi; thus the fire element is fivefold.
Regarding the samādhi of Tārā, he says:
In that regard, the collection of the wind element is Tārā,
and she is further empowered by the five Tathāgatas;
therein, the wind called *prāṇa* resides in the heart and belongs to Akṣobhya.
Apāna, located in the anus, belongs to Ratnasambhava;
Udāna, located in the throat, belongs to Amitābha; and Samāna, located in the navel, belongs to Amoghasiddhi.
Vyāna is indeed the presiding deity of all the joints; it is the abode of Vairocana.
Now, he describes the function of each of these:
"Through movement, through breath control (prāṇāyāma), and through the threads of the sense-faculties."
CMP02.036/ That which always moves forward is designated as *prāṇa*.
CMP02.037/ Because it carries away wind, urine, feces, semen, and the like,
this is always perceived by yogis as *apāna*.
That which constantly brings together everything— what is eaten, chewed, licked, drunk, and sucked— is called the *samāna* [wind],
because it moves upward, gathers [the food], and consumes what is to be eaten and enjoyed.
CMP02.042/ This [wind], conscious of the act of upward movement (udāna), through its union with knowledge, performs the functions of pervading, holding, and going and coming. CMP02.043/ Likewise,
CMP02.044/ because it pervades all the joints, it is designated as "pervasive" (vyāna).
CMP02.045: He also shows the external [elements] as fivefold:
the eastern wind belongs to Akṣobhya, and the southern wind belongs to Ratnasambhava.
The western wind is the empowerment of Amitābha, the northern wind is that of Amoghasiddhi,
and the upward wind is that of Vairocana.
The wind element has been described as fivefold.
Among these four great elements (*mahābhūta*), wherever one is present, all four are there;
therefore, they do not possess an inherent, independent, or self-established existence that is mutually unrelated.
Furthermore, because it is beyond the reach of the senses and because it is unconditioned, space is not a great element;
rather, by providing room, space performs the function of non-obstruction for all entities— this is what is meant.
CMP02.047/ Pṛthivī is known as Locanā, and the water element is remembered as Māmakī; CMP02.048/ Fire is known as Pāṇḍarā, and wind is proclaimed as Tārā—
CMP02.049/ such is the meaning of this sūtra.
CMP02.050/ Now, with reference to the meditative absorptions of the great bodhisattvas such as Kṣitigarbha and others, it is said:
CMP02.051/ Therein, the aggregate of the sense-base of the eye is Kṣitigarbha.
Furthermore, when divided into five aspects, it is empowered by the five Tathāgatas.
Therein, within the sockets of the eyes, the eye-faculty is the size of a grape; that has the nature of Akṣobhya as its pupil and of Ratnasambhava [as its white part].
The animal form is that of Amitābha;
the movement of the gaze is that of Amoghasiddhi;
the grasping of the three forms is the empowerment of Vairocana.
The sense-field of the eye has been described as fivefold. Likewise, the aggregate of the sense-field of the ear is Vajrapāṇi.
Here, within the ears, the auditory faculty consists of a collection of atoms in the form of many prominent knots; that belongs to Akṣobhya.
The nature of the ear belongs to Vairocana;
the ear canal belongs to Amitābha;
and the root of the ear belongs to Amoghasiddhi.
The apprehension of the three sounds is the empowerment of Ratnasambhava; thus it is said that the sense-base of hearing is fivefold.
CMP02.053: The aggregate of the olfactory sense-base is Ākāśagarbha.
Within the nose, the olfactory faculty (*ghrāṇendriya*) consists of a collection of atoms in the shape of a collyrium stick; it is the nature of Akṣobhya’s nose and Vairocana’s.
The middle [channel] is that of Ratnasambhava;
the nostrils are those of Amoghasiddhi;
and the apprehension of the three types of fragrance is the empowerment of Amitābha.
The fivefold sense-field of the nose has been explained.
The aggregate of the sense-field of the tongue is Lokeśvara;
therein, the tongue-faculty, which is a collection of atoms in the form of a half-moon, belongs to Akṣobhya.
The nature of the tongue belongs to Vairocana,
the root of the tongue to Ratnasambhava,
and the tip of the tongue to Amitābha.
The apprehension of the three tastes is said to be the empowerment of Amoghasiddhi; thus, the sense-field of the tongue is fivefold.
The aggregate of the sense-field of the body is Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin.
In that regard, the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*), which consists of a collection of atoms of the entire body, has the nature of Vairocana as bone,
the nature of Ratnasambhava as flesh, and [the nature] of Amitābha.
The nature of skin belongs to Amoghasiddhi;
the apprehension of the three types of touch is the empowerment of Akṣobhya— thus the fivefold sense base of the body has been described.
Regarding the *samantabhadra-samādhi*, it is said:
Here, within this body, the consciousness of the three appearances is that mental faculty (*manas-indriya*);
because it is the sovereign of all faculties, it is to be personally realized within oneself.

Because external objects do not exist, having taken the *dharmadhātu* as one's object, one brings oneself to perfection through the sequence of awakening to the *māyājāla*; endowed with all the qualities of a Buddha, one passes from Buddha-field to Buddha-field—thus is described the *samantabhadra-samādhi*.
The adamantine sense-bases (*vajrāyatana*) themselves are the supreme maṇḍala of the Bodhisattvas.
CMP02.058/ This is the meaning of this sūtra.
CMP02.059/ With reference to the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) of the deities of the sense objects,
he spoke of the ten winds.
In the *Vajramukhī-mahāyoga-tantra*, it is said:
"Namely, prāṇa, apāna, udāna, samāna, vyāna, udvāha, vivāha, saṃvāha, nirvāha, and pravāha.
Among these, the five winds beginning with prāṇa rely upon the aggregates (*skandha*) and perform the functions of the aggregates.
The five winds, beginning with *udvāha*, depend upon the sense faculties and perform the functions of the faculties.
Among them, the wind called *udvāha* depends upon the locus of the eye and accomplishes the fivefold activity of form;
furthermore, when there is the totality of light, space, mental attention, and the faculty of the eye, the object of form becomes visible.
That is the form of the erotic grace and playful charm of Vairocana, the form of the passionate affection of Akṣobhya, and [the form] of Ratnasambhava.
The form of the perception of the pleasant, the unpleasant, and equanimity belongs to Amitābha;
the form of the performance of all activities belongs to Amoghasiddhi;
thus the objective field of form has been described as fivefold.
CMP02.061: Sound, relying upon the sense-base of the ear, performs fivefold sound-activity;
therein, the sound within the ears and the sound of the hair on the head belong to Vairocana, while the sound of songs and lutes belongs to Ratnasambhava.
The sound of the palate, lips, speech, and vocal sounds is the empowerment of Amitābha;
the sound of trees, rivers, snapping fingers, clapping hands, drums, and other musical instruments is the empowerment of Amoghasiddhi;
and the sound of the syllable *hūṃ* and peaceful or wrathful utterances is the empowerment of Akṣobhya.
The object of sound has been described as fivefold.
Relying upon the nose, Saṃvāha performs the function of odor in five ways;
therein, the "entirety of odor" (aśeṣagandha) belongs to Vairocana.
The fragrance of all limbs belongs to Ratnasambhava;
the grasping of the three fragrances belongs to Amitābha;
and the fragrance of taste belongs to Amoghasiddhi.
It is said that the foul odor is the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of Akṣobhya;
thus, the object of smell is fivefold. The wind called *pravāha*, residing in the tongue, protects the fivefold object of taste.
Among those, the sweet taste belongs to Vairocana,
the astringent taste to Ratnasambhava, and the alkaline taste to Amitābha.
The pungent taste belongs to Akṣobhya;
the division of the six tastes—bitter, sour, and salty—is said to be the empowerment of Amoghasiddhi;
thus, the object of taste is fivefold.

CMP02.064: That which is called the *nirvāha* wind, residing in the sense-base of the body, accumulates strength, enthusiasm, and daring through activities such as wrestling; it maintains fivefold tactile functions.
Among these, tactile sensation while seated on a single seat belongs to Vairocana, and the tactile sensation of embracing belongs to Ratnasambhava.
The touch of kissing belongs to Amitābha;
the touch of sucking belongs to Amoghasiddhi;
and the perception of the nature of passion, dispassion, and intermediate passion arising from the touch of the union of the *bhaga* and the *liṅga* is the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of Akṣobhya.
The fivefold object of touch has been explained.
"The practitioner of mantra should always meditate upon the deity by means of form, sound, and so forth"—
this is the meaning of this aphorism.

With reference to the five wisdoms, it is said that the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*) is the simultaneous, complete knowledge of all phenomena, like seeing a reflection in a mirror; this belongs to Vairocana.

The realization that even for many beings—whether footless, two-footed, four-footed, or many-footed—all are nothing but mind (*cittamātra*) is the *samatājñāna* (knowledge of equality); this belongs to Ratnasambhava.

Having analytically distinguished and thoroughly investigated external and internal entities such as the aggregates (*skandha*) and elements (*dhātu*) individually, and having known them all to be composed of the Buddha, one contemplates all phenomena as being manifold like the petals of a lotus; dwelling thereafter without apprehension is the *pratyavekṣaṇājñāna* (knowledge of discernment), which belongs to Amitābha.

The knowledge of accomplishing activities (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*) has as its nature the fulfillment of the operations of body, speech, and mind for the sake of achieving the welfare of oneself and others; it is the purification of the obscurations of body, speech, and mind of Amoghasiddhi. The knowledge of the utterly pure realm of phenomena (*suviśuddha-dharmadhātu-jñāna*) is the liberation from birth born of karma and the purification of the latencies of conceptual constructions such as "pure" and "impure"; it is the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of Akṣobhya.
Thus it is said in the *CMP* 02.068. Therefore, he says:
The aggregates, the elements, and likewise the sense faculties—each set consisting of five—are differentiated into five.
How is it that, each one being sustained by the Tathāgatas, the karmas of saṃsāra arise?
Likewise, the five external objects, each one, are [sustained] by the five Tathāgatas.
CMP02.072–074: "Each of their own [deities] is eternally presided over; the three knowledges are based upon the five [skandhas];
thus, the families are said to be of a hundred kinds.
This is the meaning of this sūtra.
The Vajra-disciple said: "Through the lineage of a hundred families, [I have understood that] your form is composed of the atoms of all the Tathāgatas; thus, my doubt has vanished."
Furthermore, how do they become fivefold in brief?
The Vajra Master said:
The four elements bring about the formation of the bodily aggregate; through the combination of these elements, they become derivative matter (*bhautika*).
Therefore, those who belong to the lineage of the Tathāgata, consisting of the derivative matter of the aggregate of form and so forth, come to be included within the earth element.
Thus, those belonging to the Ratna family are in the water element, those belonging to the Padma family are in the fire element,
and those belonging to the Karma family are in the wind element.
Those belonging to the Vajra family are subsumed within the element of consciousness (*vijñāna-dhātu*) by this principle;

thus, in the maṇḍala of one’s own body, through the distinction between the primary elements (*bhūta*) and their derivatives (*bhautika*), the aggregates (*rāśi*) become one hundredfold, and these, in turn, consist of the five great secrets of ultimate reality (*mahātattva*).
Therefore, it is said:
In the *Śrī-guhyasamāja*, it is said:
"One should contemplate the mandala born of all vajras situated in the center of the space-element (kha-dhātu).
And one should perform the withdrawal if one desires to hold the peaceful vajra."
CMP02.080/ Illuminating this very point, he says in the *Sarvarahasyatantra*:

CMP02.081/ "The body of men is invariably seen to consist of five, being composed of the five elements alone. CMP02.082/ By cultivating their own minds—which are likewise invariably bound to the states of those [elements]—the Buddhas become manifest."
CMP02.083. It is also said in the *Khasama-tantra*:
"Behold this entire world as the nature of the five Buddhas, like a wondrous and divine drama."
CMP02.085/ For in this [state], one dances as "Great Bliss" (mahāsukha), and one [dances] with manifold flavors (anekarasa).
CMP02.086/ In brief, however, it is fivefold.
CMP02.087/ Such is the meaning of this sūtra.
The Vajra-disciple asked:
"Furthermore, how do the five aspects come to possess a threefold nature?"
The Vajra-Guru Ratnasambhava said: "One becomes non-dual with the Body-Vajra;
Amoghasiddhi becomes non-dual with the Speech-Vajra."
Akṣobhya becomes non-dual with the sixth Tathāgata;
thus, beginning from the hundred families up to those consisting of the five families, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are subsumed within one’s own body, speech, and mind,
as stated by the Blessed One in the *Śrī-Guhyasamāja-mahāyoga-tantra*.
CMP02.090. Then all those Tathāgatas caused their own body, speech, and mind to enter into the syllables of the three Vajrasattvas.
CMP02.091. Through the contemplation of body, speech, and mind, no intrinsic nature is perceived.
CMP02.092. By means of the application of the mantra-form, there is neither awakening nor meditation.
CMP02.093–094: Having briefly investigated this characteristic of body, speech, and mind, one should meditate upon the samādhi of the union with awakening (*bodhi*) as conceived through mantra.
Thus, in the *Śrī-sarvabuddhasamāyoga-ḍākinījālasaṃvara-mahāyogatantra*, illuminating this very point, it is said:
Yoga does not arise with respect to reflected images or cast statues;
rather, through the great yoga of the *bodhicitta*, the deities are the yogin himself. Indeed, one’s own self is all-buddhahood and all-heroism.
CMP02.099/ Therefore, through union with one's own presiding deity, one should accomplish [the goal] by means of the self alone.
CMP02.100/ Furthermore, they attain a threefold nature through the application of body, speech, and mind.
CMP02.101/ Such is the meaning of this sūtra.
The Vajra-disciple said:
"I am free from doubt that the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, who consist of all families, are subsumed within one's own body, speech, and mind."
Furthermore, how do the three families become the Body-Vajra, whose nature is indivisible from the three vajras? Speak, Blessed One; speak, Vajraguru, the Teacher!
(CMP 2.103) Vajraguru said:
Excellent, excellent, O Mahāsattva! For the benefit of those gathered here, you inquire about the ultimate limit of the isolation of the body.
Therefore, listen as I demonstrate to you how body, speech, and mind are the mutual causes of one another, and I shall establish you in the vajra-body samādhi.
"One who is impelled by the mantra-contemplation of body, speech, and mind shall accomplish the supreme siddhi, which is dear to the satisfaction of the mind. Thus [it is said].
The Blessed One has stated this in the *Śrīguhyasamāja*:

"The intention here is that when there is the Holder of the Body-Vajra (*kāyavajradhara*), the activity of the Speech-Vajra (*vāgvajra*) occurs upon obtaining the complete assembly of the tongue within the cavity of the palate and lips."
In that regard, the mind-vajra (citta-vajra) acts as the impeller;
thus, through the union of the three vajras, one should accomplish the siddhi that brings joy to the mind—this is the meaning.
Having thus defined the characteristic of the inseparability of body, speech, and mind:
Now, the characteristic of the indivisibility of the three vajras is established:
"May you generate the mind in the form of the body, the body in the form of the mind, and the mind through the utterance of speech.
Thus it was said in the *Śrī-Guhyasamāja*.

Having generated firmness within oneself by thinking, "I am pure by nature," one should resolve that one's own self is Mahāvajradhara, whose nature is indivisible from the three vajras; this is called the yoga of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna-yoga*).
This concludes the second chapter, the resolution of doubts concerning the isolation of body (*kāya-viveka*) and its integration (*melāvana*).
Chapter III: The Section on the Resolution of Doubts Concerning the Union of the Discrimination of Speech.
Vajra-śiṣya said:
Having become free from doubt regarding the training in physical seclusion, [the disciple asks:
"O Blessed One, Teacher, Vajra-Guru, tell us: how should one train in verbal seclusion? How should one practice it?"
The Vajra Master said:
"Excellent, excellent, O Great Being!

This body isolation (*kāya-viveka*) of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), sense-bases (*āyatana*), and so forth, which was just described, as well as the placement of the deities therein, is common to all because it is the coarse yoga."

The discernment of speech, however, is the extremely subtle knowledge of yogins; it is not the domain of Mahāyāna practitioners, nor is it the sphere of those following the generation stage (utpattikrama) of the Vajrayāna, because it is a subtle yoga.
Therefore, listen with diligence: I shall awaken you to the samādhi of the Speech-Vajra by means of a detailed explanation according to the *Vyākhyātantra*.
CMP03.003: "In that regard, the families are said to be of a hundred kinds," and so forth; this previously mentioned sūtra is common even to the isolation (*viveka*) of body, speech, and mind.
Among these, what is called the isolation of speech is the reality (*tattva*) of mantra, and that is not known without the sequential order of the reality of breath (*vāyu*).
The *vāyu-tattva* is indeed breath control (*prāṇāyāma*).
Therefore, the introductory passage for the *vāyu-tattva* is extracted from the *Śrī-guhyasamāja*:
"The great jewel of five colors, the size of a mustard seed. (CMP 3.4)
CMP03.005–006: "One should always cultivate [the deity] at the tip of the nose with effort through yoga.
This *vajrapada* is twofold according to the distinction between the interpretable (*neyārtha*) and the definitive (*nītārtha*), and it also applies to the yoga of the two types of deities.

In that regard, for the practitioner of the generation stage (*utpattikrama*), the instruction on subtle yoga is as follows: one should cultivate at the tip of the nose a symbol of one's own deity the size of a mustard seed, in order to stabilize one's own mind.

CMP03.007: By this very [method], he explains the subtle yoga for those who have attained the meditative absorption of the completion stage (*niṣpannakrama*): having produced the three syllables in the form of female, male, and neuter through the vowels (*āli*) and consonants (*kāli*), and having applied those three syllables to the stages of entry, abiding, and emergence, one should perform the *vajrajāpa*, which consists of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), according to the sequence of the four mandalas.
CMP03.008/ Illuminating this point, he says:

CMP03.009/ Having emitted the breath, which consists of the five wisdoms and has the nature of the five elements, CMP03.010/ one should visualize it in the form of a single mass at the tip of the lotus-nose.
CMP03.011/ The great jewel of five colors is known as *prāṇāyāma*.
CMP03.012/ This was stated in the *Samājottara*.
CMP03.013/ He now states the detailed explanation (*nirdeśa*) of these summary points (*uddeśapada*).

CMP 03.014–015: Then the Blessed One, the Great Vajrin, having properly prostrated to the sole Teacher of the World, replied to him who was speaking on the meaning of vajra-recitation (*vajrajāpa*) within the *Sandhyāvyākaraṇasamājavyākhyātantra*.
CMP03.016/ This awakening mind (bodhicitta) has been revealed as merely worldly scripture. CMP03.017/ How indeed will future followers understand it as supramundane?
CMP03.018/ For the Dharma was taught by you for the sake of abandoning all views.
CMP03.019: How then is that bodhicitta, which is that very view, made well-firm?
CMP03.020: Those who are deluded by intentional (sandhyāya) speech do not understand the stated meaning; CMP03.021: they grasp it according to the literal expression and say, "It is not otherwise."
CMP03.022. Then the Blessed One Viśva said to Vajrapāṇi:
CMP03.023. "Excellent, excellent, O Lord of Secrets! You have prophesied those who will come in the future.
CMP03.024. The thought of awakening (bodhicitta) becomes the wind, and it is established in space."
CMP03.025/ And being the life-force of sentient beings, consisting of five and designated as ten, CMP03.026/ that which is called the twelvefold dependent origination is by its very nature a triad;
CMP03.027/ this, known as wind, is the preeminent among all the senses, the very essence of the mind of awakening (bodhicitta).

CMP03.028–030: That which is unmanifest and subtle is always said to be manifest. Because of its support, people perform actions such as those concerning sense objects, as well as rites for pacification, nourishment, subjugation, and malevolent magic.
CMP03.031 But all that [arises] from the *bodhicitta*, which is the locus and support for the three principles (*tri-tattva*).
CMP03.032 Likewise, however many various worldly conventions are imagined,
CMP03.033 they always arise from the *bodhicitta* as conceptualizations, like the wind.
CMP03.034/ Phenomena such as pleasure and pain are produced from the seed alone;
CMP03.035/ this has the nature of bodhicitta and is like the non-dual void of the aggregates and so forth.
CMP03.036/ Through the single union of wisdom and means, the world becomes bodhicitta.
CMP03.037. The Lord himself should utter [the mantra], free from meditation and study.
CMP03.038. Through the division of day and night, by means of the application of the moon and sun, CMP03.039.
the exhalation indeed pervades the world—the singular wind of the *bodhicitta*.
CMP03.040/ Having abandoned the fruits of the auspicious and inauspicious, one indeed becomes like the sky.
CMP03.041/ The Vajra-disciple said:
It was stated that the wind is fivefold and has ten designations.
"Out of compassion, O Blessed One, please speak of the different designations for each of the winds.
The Vajra Guru replied:
"We shall demonstrate that which has been indicated by the very tantra of the explanation just mentioned."

CMP03.043. Then the Blessed One, having likewise entered into all the Tathāgatas and all the Bodhisattvas for the sake of pleasing them, spoke these ten winds of the Lord of Tathāgatas: CMP03.044–045. Those known as prāṇa, apāna, and samāna; those designated as udāna and vyāna; and [the five] nāga, kūrma, kṛkara, devadatta, and dhanañjaya.
CMP03.046/ Having made these [winds] one's own image, one again creates the form of a woman.

CMP03.047/ These ten winds, which have been taught in various languages according to the system of the *Śrī-sarvabuddhasamāyoga-ḍākinījālasaṃvara*, he also states as follows: CMP03.048/ Koṭākhyah, Koṭavah, Koṭaḥ, Koṭābhaḥ, and Kaṭīrakaḥ.

CMP03.049/ Kolākhyah, kolavaḥ, kolaḥ, kolābhaḥ, and likewise kaliḥ; CMP03.050/ these ten names are taught as the ten winds according to their literal meaning in the *Vajramukhī-mahāyoga-tantra*: namely, prāṇa, apāna, udāna, samāna, vyāna, udvāha, vivāha, saṃvāha, pravāha, and nirvāha.
CMP03.051/ The Vajra-disciple said: "O Blessed One, Teacher, O Vajra-guru, tell me: where do the ten winds, beginning with prāṇa, reside within this body, and what do they do?"
The Vajra-Guru said:
"The five winds, abiding in the divisions of the body, perform the functions of the body;
the five winds, abiding in the sense-bases such as the eye, perform the functions of the faculties."
In that regard, the *prāṇa* residing in the heart is the Tathāgata Akṣobhya; the *apāna* residing in the anus is the Tathāgata Ratnasambhava;
and the *udāna* residing in the throat is the Tathāgata Amitābha.
The Tathāgata Amoghasiddhi is the *samāna* wind located in the navel;
the Tathāgata Vairocana is the *vyāna* wind located in all the joints.
Thus, the upward movement is form (*rūpa*).
Marriage is sound, union is fragrance,
and flow is taste.
Carrying away (nirvāha) and touch (sparśa)—
these are the ten winds; furthermore, they become inhalation and exhalation,
and they further consist of the four mandalas beginning with Vāyavya.
Furthermore, they consist of the four goddesses;
furthermore, they consist of the five elements;
and furthermore, they consist of the five cognitions, such as the mirror-like wisdom and so forth.
Furthermore, they consist of the five rays beginning with white;
furthermore, they consist of the nature of the five Tathāgatas;
and furthermore, having become the support for the three syllables, they perform the vajra-recitation through the sequence of entry, abiding, and emergence.
Furthermore, those winds, having become the support for the letter A, cause the utterance of all speech without exception;
and furthermore, having pervaded the unstruck sound (*anāhata*), they become devoid of intrinsic nature.
The Vajra-disciple said:
“Blessed One, how do these ten winds, through a nature both single and manifold, perform the radiation and reabsorption within one’s own body day and night?
Speak, Blessed One, Vajra Guru, Teacher!
The Vajra Guru replied:

Excellent, excellent, O Mahāsattva! In the *Śrītattvasaṅgraha* and other such root tantras (*mūlatantra*), as well as in the higher tantras (*uttaratantra*), the reality of wind (*vāyutattva*) has not been clearly stated because it was spoken in intentional language (*saṃdhyābhāṣita*). However, in the explanatory tantras (*vyākhyātantra*), it is spoken according to the literal sense; that [teaching] shall now be introduced.
Arising from the nostrils, abiding in the families of the five Buddhas,
the movement of the five winds constantly circulates within the body;
its conventional flow issues forth from that gateway.
CMP03.060/ These are of four types: left, right, both together, and motionless.
CMP03.061/ From the right [nostril], the element of extension (prasaras) indeed proceeds as the fire-maṇḍala;
CMP03.062/ this clearly manifests as red in color and moves as the Lord of the Lotus (Padmanātha).
CMP03.063/ From the left side, the element that flows forth emerges from the wind mandala;
CMP03.064/ it moves as the karma-nātha, appearing greenish-dark in color.
CMP03.065/ The element that flows forth from the pair is similar in appearance to the color of gold.
CMP03.066/ The Māhendra-maṇḍala indeed moves for Ratnanātha;
CMP03.067/ the element is motionless and not expansive; in an instant, the Vāruṇa-maṇḍala, CMP03.068/ resembling pure crystal, moves for Vajranātha.
Having extracted all the elements (dhātu), supported by the relationship of the container and the contained,
the great body of Vairocana shall emerge at the end of death.
One should always recite this four-maṇḍala while remaining in meditative equipoise.
CMP03.072–073: "Day and night, the mantra should always be recited by the practitioners according to the prescribed number of recitations.
This was stated by the Blessed One in the *Vajramālā-mahāyoga-tantra*;
this is its meaning.
From the two nostrils of the vajra and the lotus, one should emit rays of light;
having gone upward from the tip of the conventional nose, they issue forth in the sequence of left, right, both, and the steady [central] breath.
In this regard, the procedure is as follows:
The wind emerging from the left nostril is the Tathāgata Amoghasiddhi;
its nature is wind, the wind mandala, having the form of greenish-black rays.
The wind circulating from the right nostril is the Tathāgata Amitābha.
The fire-maṇḍala, which has the nature of heat and the nature of red rays, issues forth from the pair of nostrils; the wind is Ratnasambhava, the Indra-maṇḍala, having the nature of yellow rays;
and the wind that is still and of slow movement is Akṣobhya.
The nature of the water element is the white light ray, which is the Varuṇa-maṇḍala;
the four elemental maṇḍalas are pervaded by the pervasive wind (vyāna), and the light ray does not issue forth—the Tathāgata Śrī-Vairocana is of a nature equal to space (kha-sama).
Nevertheless, each individual light ray would indeed issue forth.
Five rays of light emerge from each [deity];
since the four elements are pervaded by a single element-maṇḍala,
the sovereign of the three-syllable mantra should himself constantly recite [the mantra] within each individual maṇḍala according to the sequence of entry and so forth.
The reality of wind has been explained in brief.
The Vajra-disciple said:
"By the grace of the Guru's feet, I have been well-instructed in the reality of wind through both scripture and realization."
"Now, desiring to know the definition of the reality of mantra,
may the Blessed One, the Teacher, the Vajra-Guru, out of compassion, explain it.
The Vajra-Guru said:

Excellent, excellent, Mahāsattva! Regarding that which is called the reality of mantra (*mantra-tattva*), although only the mantras themselves were uttered in the *Tattvasaṃgraha* and other root tantras (*mūla-tantra*) as well as in the explanatory tantras (*uttara-tantra*), the extraction of the mantras (*mantroddhāra*) was not demonstrated there.

However, in the Explanatory Tantra (*vyākhyā-tantra*), the Blessed One has revealed with perfect clarity the extraction of the mantras, the symbolic code of the mantras (*mantra-saṅketa*), the meaning of the mantras, and the reality of the mantras.
Therefore, those who have not mastered the Explanatory Tantra and are devoted only to external mantras do not understand this.
Therefore, listen with diligence; according to the explanatory tantras, I shall awaken you to the reality of mantras.
Among them, the mantras of the serpents and others arise from *ālikāli*;
their reality is the three-syllabled [mantra] born from the *anāhata*.

Since all mantras— whether feminine, masculine, or neuter in nature— enter into the three syllables according to the instructions as they were received, the three syllables are the sovereign of all mantras;
furthermore, each of those [mantras] is produced by three syllables together with the Unstruck (anāhata).
CMP03.079: Now the function of the three syllables is described.
In that regard, first, through the union of the three, one brings forth the form of the deity;
that very [form] sustains the body day and night through the sequence of entry, abiding, and emergence.

That very [element], together with the vowels and consonants (*ālikāli*), at the time of the union of the two organs, turns face downwards; having emerged from the aperture of the secret nose in the form of semen, it generates the realms of sentient beings.

That same [element], together with *prāṇāyāma*, ascends once again, awakens the gateway of the sense organs, and emerging through the gateway of the conventional nose in the sequence of left, right, and so forth, performs the effortless *vajrajāpa* and purifies previous karmic obscurations.

By means of the sequence of days and nights, he observes the count of recitations; relying on colors such as white during the arising of the mandalas of Varuṇa and the others, he performs all rites, such as those for pacification.

He performs the recitation by means of the characteristic of "vocal recitation"—which is conceptualized in the form of syllables but not produced by the movement of the tip of the tongue—and having performed it, he relies on external activities such as the use of colors and so forth to perform all rites, such as those for pacification.
By means of the sequence of purifying, awakening, and inflaming the three syllables, he purifies food and renders it free from disease.

Having performed everything in this manner while in the state of the physical body, and finally having entered the *anāhata* [unstruck sound], one again assumes an ordinary body and performs everything exactly as before.
Now, the Blessed One speaks of the arising of the three syllables in the *Sandhyāvyākaraṇamahāyogatantra*:

CMP03.081/ One who is not bound by the ten [vowels] among those from one up to nine; CMP03.082/ one should know him to be unbound; he knows the supreme state. CMP03.083/ The vowels, consonants, and phonemes follow the number nine.
He who knows that there is no mutual conjunction between the bound and the other is the teacher of the world.
He who, having understood this, desires the perfection consisting of the fruit of liberation,
attains that very state which is formless and devoid of form.

CMP03.087–089: [The mantra] is joined with the end of the elements (bhūtānta) and situated in the sixteenth [digit], beginning with the kalās. It is conjoined with five groups of five, and arranged in four and three;
it possesses the anusvāra and the long vowels, and is subject to the rules of vowel qualities (guṇa), conjunctions (saṃyoga), and elision (lopa).
CMP03.090: The entire sentence should be short; it is neither manifold nor singular.
CMP03.091: Whatever is to be accomplished for the sake of the letter *ya* by one desiring success, CMP03.092:
the activity of the world proceeds by means of that very triad beginning with the letter *ra*.
Those phonemes which have been described as being at the back and those which are facing forward—
whether feminine, masculine, or neuter— are conceived as the beginning of the *dhātus*.
Having understood them as joined above and below, they are applied by means of the intellect.
CMP03.096/ It is said that by means of the six [perfections], one produces the four, three, and one [realities] born from the state of being without intrinsic nature and the single nature.
CMP03.097/ Having applied those to the object of the "Yā" syllable and so forth, the knowledge of the three times arises.
CMP03.098/ Like a dream or a magical illusion, the wise one should act within the world of the three realms.
CMP03.099/ This mantra, which arises from the nature of the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva-svabhāva*), is that which is uttered.
CMP03.100/ From that, the manifested form which is the perception of the deity [arises].
CMP03.101/ It is conventional (*sāṅketika*), established in the three principles (*tri-tattva*), and characterized by natural recitation (*prakṛti-jāpa*).
CMP03.102 This supreme bodhicitta is ineffable and inexpressible.
CMP03.103 That very [bodhicitta] is the unity of the triad; it is without departure and without arrival, CMP03.104 without cessation, utterly tranquil, and free from eternalism and nihilism.

CMP03.105–107: The knower of yoga, in all activities such as sitting and so forth, [should contemplate] that which is characterized by the resolution formed through the knowledge of the three times, which has the characteristic of non-difference from space, which is indeed ultimate, and which has the characteristic of being personally realized within oneself.
CMP03.108/ One should always recite that which is inexpressible, unutterable, and transcendent of the three times.
CMP03.109/ The recitation of Pāṇḍarā and the others is said to be two hundred and twenty-five [per day].
CMP03.110/ When correctly multiplied by four, it becomes nine hundred and four, which is the fourfold yoga.
CMP03.111/ That which is seen as nine hundred through twenty-four circumambulations,
CMP03.112/ from its production, becomes two hundred and sixteen thousand;
CMP03.113/ thus, in the *Guhyasandhi*, the subtle yoga has been revealed.
CMP03.114/ But even that which is devoid of meditation and study is called *japa*.
CMP03.115/ Thus, the reality of the internal mantra is explained.
CMP03.116: The Vajra-disciple said:
"I am free from doubt regarding the cause for the manifestation of the syllables of internal speech;
however, it was stated by the Blessed One that the short [vowel] constitutes the entirety of speech. How, then, does the short *a* become the cause for the manifestation of all speech?"
The Vajra Master said:
"Excellent, excellent, Great Being!
Here, those who follow the scriptures prioritize grammar and merely recollect the literal meaning of the words."

However, they do not understand the reality of syllables as it truly is— namely, where, from what cause, and in what manner syllables and verbal expressions arise— because this is the domain of the Buddhas. Listen, and I shall awaken you according to the teaching.
CMP03.118: Sound (*śabda*), first of all, consists of *āli* and *kāli*. *Āli* refers to the sixteen vowels beginning with *a*, and *kāli* refers to the thirty-three consonants beginning with *ka*.

That which is joined with the sixteen vowels and consists of forty-nine letters—comprising all sounds whether separate or combined, including vowels, consonants, *bindu*, *visarga*, *saṃhitā*, verbal roots, case endings, compounds, word analysis, feminine gender, verbal terminations (*tiṅanta*), primary suffixes (*kṛt*), secondary suffixes (*taddhita*), and so forth, up to the commentaries—is known by the technical designation and convention of the name "Grammar" (*vyākaraṇa*).

Therefore, from that [source], there arise the eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dharma (*dharma-skandha*), including sūtras, tantras, rituals (*kalpa*), the Tripiṭaka, poetry, dramas, and so forth— comprising worldly and transcendent treatises (*śāstra*) consisting of words, sentences, meters, prosody, verses, stanzas, and *daṇḍakas*.
Relying upon these treatises, all accomplishments (*siddhi*) are attained,
as stated by the Blessed One in the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*.

CMP03.119: "For example, Mahāmati, just as a certain person might take a lamp and search for wealth, even so, Mahāmati, by means of the lamp of the sounds of verbal conceptualization, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas enter into the state of personal realization that is free from verbal conceptualization. CMP03.120:
"However, this letter 'A' is the consciousness of those specific phonemes contained within words, sentences, and so forth."
Because consonants such as *ka* and so forth do not exist apart from the vowel *a*, and because they are consonantal (*halanta*), they are not expressible [as independent entities],
as stated by the Blessed One in the *Nāmasaṅgīti*:

The letter A is the foremost of all phonemes, of great significance, and the supreme syllable; it is indeed the great vital breath, unarisen, and devoid of vocal expression and utterance; it is the foremost cause of all verbal designations and the perfect luminosity of all speech.
Then it was said by the Blessed One: "The syllable A is the seed-syllable for the gateway to all meditations, because all phenomena are unproduced from the very beginning.
Furthermore, it is called the innate syllable (sahajākṣara).
In the *Vajramaṇḍalālaṅkāra-tantra* as well, illuminating the syllable A, it says:
"The unstruck (*anāhata*) in the center of the heart, blazing like a lamp, the supreme imperishable syllable, the syllable A, the supreme Lord. (CMP 03.125–126)

CMP03.127–128: Thus, all the Tathāgatas, having known as it truly is that speech—which has the letter *a* as its lineage, has the letter *a* as its cause, is born from the letter *a*, is by nature perishing as soon as it is uttered, and is characterized by the conceptualization of words—is independent of correct or incorrect sounds, they teach the Dharma to those to be trained according to the differences in the dispositions and latent tendencies of sentient beings.
Therefore, it was said by the Blessed One in the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*:
"O Mahāmati, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should rely upon the meaning."
Mahāmati, a son of good family or a daughter of good family who follows after the letter and relies upon the letter destroys themselves and does not cause others to understand the ultimate truth.
CMP03.130. For example, Mahāmati, suppose someone were to show something to another person with a finger, and that person were to pursue only the tip of the finger for the sake of seeing;

in just this way, Mahāmati, those of a childish nature—the classes of foolish common people—will pass away while remaining attached to the literal meaning, like those who cling to the tip of the finger.

They do not abandon the ultimate meaning to pursue the literal sense, like the tip of a finger; therefore, those who seek the true meaning should serve them, while those who are the opposite— those who are attached to the literal meaning— should be avoided by one seeking the true meaning.
CMP03.132/ Furthermore, it was stated by the Blessed One in this very sūtra that the engagement of speech is also fourfold.
CMP03.133/ Mahāmati, the characteristic of the conceptualization of speech is fourfold; namely:
speech characterized by [conceptual] marks, dream-speech, and speech based on the adherence to depravity.

In this regard, Mahāmati, speech arising from conceptualization since beginningless time consists of the speech of characteristics, which proceeds from attachment to the signs and forms of one's own conceptualization;
furthermore, Mahāmati, dream-speech proceeds from the recollection of previously experienced objects and from the absence of any currently bound object.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, speech characterized by the attachment to the conceptualization of depravity proceeds from the recollection of the past karma of sentient beings. Furthermore, Mahāmati, speech characterized by conceptualization from beginningless time proceeds from the latencies of the seeds of one's own depravity due to the attachment to the proliferation of conceptualization (*prapañca*) since beginningless time.
Indeed, Mahāmati, this is the fourfold characteristic of the conceptualization of speech.
CMP03.134: By this principle, sound (*śabda*) is "syllable" (*akṣara*) because it arises from the letter *a*;
"perishable" (*kṣara*) means destruction, while "imperishable" (*akṣara*) means non-destruction. That which has the nature of being equal to space is that which is established by means of sound.
That very completion stage (*niṣpannakrama*) is also unconditioned, having a nature that is without beginning or end,
as it is said in the *Ekanayanirdeśasūtra* (CMP 03.135):
"These phenomena are designated by means of verbal sounds, yet neither phenomena nor sound are found here."
CMP03.136/ And having entered into the oneness of the way, one will touch the supreme, excellent patience that is the nature of phenomena (dharmatā).
CMP03.137/ As it is said in the *Vairocanābhisambodhi-caryā-tantra*:
CMP03.138/ "Moreover, O Lord of Secrets, the characteristic of mantras was not created by all the Buddhas, nor caused to be created, nor approved."

For what reason? It is because this is the true nature (*dharmatā*) of these phenomena: whether Tathāgatas arise or whether Tathāgatas do not arise, this true nature of phenomena remains constant; that is to say, the true nature of mantras is the mantra-nature.
In this regard, O Lord of the Guhyakas, there exists a spell (*vidyā*) called Madayantikā belonging to the Lord of the Desire Realm.
By means of that [power], she intoxicates all the sons of the gods belonging to the desire realm with pride,
displays various and diverse delightful regions,
and having manifested various and diverse objects of enjoyment, she bestows them upon the gods who wield power over the creations of others (paranirmita-vaśavartin) and enjoys them herself.
CMP03.141: For example, the divine son Maheśvara possesses a spell called *manojava* (swift as thought);

by means of it, he performs every task within the triple-thousand great-thousandfold world system, and having magically produced all manner of enjoyments and articles of luxury, he bestows them upon the gods of the Śuddhāvāsa realm and partakes of them himself.
CMP03.142: For example, just as a master illusionist displays various and diverse objects such as humans by means of mantras—
just as he displays an illusion by means of mantras,
or just as he removes poison and fevers and the like by means of mantras— so it is here.
Just as, for example, a deity who possesses the power of mantras bestows welfare upon sentient beings through those mantras;
or just as, for example, by means of mantras the heat of fire is destroyed and coolness arises—
by these illustrative examples, the power of mantras is to be firmly believed in.
And that power of the mantra indeed does not emerge from the mantra, nor does it enter into sentient beings,
nor is it perceived in the practitioner.
Moreover, noble son, the manifestation of the nature of reality through the empowerment of mantras does not transcend the three times,
because it is in every respect produced by inconceivable dependent origination.
CMP03.144: Therefore, O son of noble family, one who has attained the realization of the nature of inconceivable phenomena should constantly and continuously follow the way of mantra.

CMP03.145: Having thus established through scripture and realization the inconceivable power of internal and external jewels, mantras, and medicinal herbs, he now speaks, demonstrating the purification of speech as it truly is for the realms of beings, both those who have reached perfection and those who have not.
In the *Kinnararājaparipṛcchā-sūtra*:
"Furthermore, O Lord of Kinnaras, from where do the sounds and voices of all sentient beings issue forth?
He replied:

"Son of good family, from space the cries and sounds of all sentient beings issue forth. He replied, "But, Lord of Kinnaras, do the cries and sounds of all sentient beings not also issue forth from their internal cavities?"
CMP03.149: He said:
"What do you think, son of good family? Do the sounds and cries of all sentient beings issue forth from the internal cavity of the body, or rather from the mind?"
He said,
"O Lord of the Kinnaras, it is neither from the body nor from the mind; for what reason?"
For the body is indeed insentient and motionless, resembling grass, a wall, wood, or a reflection;
and the mind, too, is invisible, like an illusion, non-obstructive, and non-informative. Thus it was said.
Furthermore, son of good family, from what else could sounds emerge that are entirely free from body and mind?
He replied:
"O Lord of Kinnaras, the communication of sounds by all sentient beings arises from space and from non-mental engagement."
CMP03.153: He said:
"What do you think, son of good family? If space did not exist, from where would sounds emerge? CMP03.154: He replied:
"O Lord of Kinnaras, there is no utterance whatsoever that is separate from space.
[He said:
"Therefore, noble son, by this very method it should be understood thus."
Whatever vocal activities emerge,
they all emerge from space;
for sounds have the nature of space, and as soon as they have issued forth, they cease.
And once ceased, they abide in nothing other than the very nature of space;
all phenomena have been declared to be of the nature of space, and whether they are expressed or unexpressed,
they do not deviate from that very equality with the limit of space.
For, son of good family, all phenomena are mere sounds; they are to be communicated through non-communication, yet they are expressed by means of conventional designations.
And that conventional expression is no convention at all. For whatever convention is expressed by means of sounds and designations does not adhere to any phenomenon whatsoever.

CMP03.157: Thus, the great yogin, established in the samādhi of the vajra of speech, having heard statements consisting of descriptions of the faults and virtues of both perfected and unperfected realms of sentient beings, is neither attached,
nor drawn back, nor terrified.

He is neither terrified nor does he doubt; likewise, having heard the various compositions of words such as worldly and transcendent treatises, *daṇḍakas*, *troṭakas*, and so forth, he is not attracted, not repelled, and not deluded, because he has reached the ultimate range of all sounds.
As it was said by the Blessed One in the *Sarvadharmāpravṛttinirdeśasūtra*:

"O son of the gods, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is established in the entry into the sounds and cries [of all beings] were to be reviled and abused with false and unreal words for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges, no thought of resentment would arise in him."

If one were to honor, revere, respect, and worship [the Buddha] for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges, providing all the requisites of happiness—robes, alms-food, bedding and seats, and medicinal provisions for the sick—that person would not give rise to a mind of attachment therein.

Likewise, the mantra-practitioner who dwells in the Vajra-speech samādhi and has attained mastery on the eighth stage is neither afflicted nor captivated by gain or loss, fame or infamy, blame or praise, or pleasure and pain.
Therefore, having overcome all worldly conditions and transcended the sequence of birth, one who desires to seek the isolation of the mind attends upon a spiritual friend.
This concludes the third chapter: The Severing of Doubts Concerning the Union with the Isolation of Speech.
Chapter IV: The Section on Resolving Doubts Concerning the Integration of Mental Isolation.
Vajra-disciple said:

"By the grace of the Guru’s feet, having become free from doubt regarding the reality of the winds (*vāyu-tattva*) in its successive stages and regarding the discrimination of speech (*vāg-viveka*) within the reality of mantra (*mantra-tattva*), I now desire to train in the discrimination of the mind (*citta-viveka*). For the benefit of those with deep conviction, may the Blessed One, the Vajra-Guru Teacher, explain how one trains.
The Vajra-Guru said:

"Excellent, excellent, Mahāsattva! You inquire about the domain of the Buddhas—which is beyond the reach of those who look outward from the tradition of all the Tathāgatas, which is exceedingly profound and extremely difficult to fathom—because it has been stated by the Blessed One in every scriptural teaching that the intrinsic nature of the mind is rootless, non-abiding, without a locus, without marks, without color, without shape, beyond the senses, and not the domain of logicians. Therefore, desiring Buddhahood, one should rely upon the Vajrayāna, propitiate a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), and investigate the intrinsic nature of one's own mind."
As it was said by the Blessed One in the *Śrī-tattvasaṃgraha-tantra*:
"O son of noble family, practice through the meditative concentration of observing one's own mind";
and the *Śrī-vairocanābhisambodhi-tantra* also says:
It is also stated in the system of the Three Baskets that awakening is the thorough knowledge of one's own mind as it truly is:
"Far-reaching, moving alone, bodiless, dwelling in the cave. (CMP 4.4)
CMP04.005/ "Those who settle the mind are liberated from the bonds of Māra.

CMP04.006/ For this reason, one who desires to realize the illusion-like samādhi (*māyopama-samādhi*) should abandon all obscurations of distraction and, having propitiated the Vajra-gurus who have received the oral transmission of all the Tathāgatas,
should realize the threefold consciousness as the manifestation of intrinsic nature (*prakṛty-ābhāsa*), in accordance with the explanatory tantras such as the *Śrī-jñānavajra-samuccaya*.
As it was said by the Blessed One in the Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra:

"Furthermore, Mahāmati, a bodhisattva who wishes to thoroughly understand the range of the conceptual construction of the perceived and the perceiver— which is the manifestation of one's own mind— must be free from the hindrances of socializing, worldly association, and drowsiness."

CMP04.008. In this regard, all entities that serve as the causes for the threefold consciousness—namely, heaven and liberation; the stationary and the moving; the grasped and the grasper; the wheel of twelve-linked dependent origination; the conceptualization of the auspicious and the inauspicious; light and darkness; the forms of female, male, and neuter, and so forth; birth, abiding, and dissolution; and, in brief, the triple world which is the domain of the investigation of the faculties—these constitute the threefold consciousness, as stated by the Blessed One in the *Bhadrapāliparipṛcchā-sūtra*.
The Blessed One said:
"Bhadrapāla, that mechanism which operates through the predominance of karma is produced by consciousness in accordance with that karma."
In the very same way, the machine of the body functions due to the predominance of consciousness;
this element of consciousness proceeds with diverse and wondrous activities,
and this element of consciousness is the agent.

Because it is the agent that produces the body, this element of consciousness (vijñāna-dhātu) is imperishable; because it cultivates the realm of phenomena (dharma-dhātu), this element of consciousness is endowed with intelligence;
and because it recollects its former bodily supports, this element of consciousness is perfected in wisdom.
Furthermore, this element of consciousness (vijñāna-dhātu) should be viewed as being like the rays of the sun.

For example, just as the rays of the sun fall upon foul-smelling impurities and corpses, as well as upon fragrant things such as lotuses, yet they do not come into contact with their fragrance; so it is with this.
Nor does it transfer to the sun because of its freedom from foul odors;
in the same way, this consciousness-element (vijñāna-dhātu) takes up rebirth even among those such as pigs who feed on excrement and filth,
yet the consciousness-element is not defiled by those faults.
CMP04.011. Then Mahauṣadhi, prostrating at the feet of the Blessed One, addressed the Blessed One as follows:
"Blessed One, what is the nature of consciousness when it has departed from the body?
CMP04.012. The Blessed One said:
"Excellent, excellent, Mahauṣadhi! It is just as you have now questioned me; I shall explain it to you.
