CMP09.047–049: "By those very things through which the deluded are bound and destroyed in the vicinity of Raurava, they are indeed liberated with ease through the power of wisdom.

By this principle, since a distinguished fruit is accomplished through distinguished superimposition and distinguished transformation, there is no other means for attaining the fruit of unsurpassed great bliss than that which has entered into the state of being the cause.
For that purpose, by means of those very same qualities— such as pleasant food, conduct, and so forth— the perfection of omniscience, including the eightfold sovereign powers and other attributes,
is brought to manifestation. Therefore, it is stated in the *Śrīsaṃvara* that the state of all-buddhahood is attained through happiness by means of happiness itself.
CMP09.052. Therein, the bodhisattva conduct born of passion is threefold, namely:
conceptual proliferation (*prapañcatā*), non-proliferation (*niṣprapañcatā*), and absolute non-proliferation (*atyanta-niṣprapañcatā*).
Among these, what is conduct characterized by conceptual proliferation?
Namely, as it is taught in the *Tathāgatāśvāsa* and the *Vajradharāśvāsa*, the extensive *āralli* of all the Tathāgatas—that is *prapañca*.
What is *niṣprapañca*?
It is when, by virtue of a continuous and pervasive activity, there might be an *āralli* in a particular instance; that is *niṣprapañca*.
What is absolute non-proliferation (*atyanta-niṣprapañcatā*)?

Having abandoned all attachments, dwelling on the nourishment of solitary meditation, one should practice through the meditative absorption of the Knowledge-Seal (*jñāna-mudrā*). That is absolute non-proliferation;
it is like wood that, when burned, becomes ash.
It burns the palm leaf and becomes ash;
it burns the cotton and becomes ash;
everything is reduced to ashes.
In this very way, through the three types of conduct, they accomplish the state of Mahāvajradhara.

Now, certain practitioners who follow tantras such as the *Tattvasaṃgraha* achieve the siddhi of Mahāmudrā through the practice of elaborate conduct (*prapañcacaryā*) day and night, with minds constantly engaged in the application of hand-gestures (*hasta-mudrā*), songs, offerings, dramatic gestures, and the dancing of actors and dancers.

Likewise, some, relying on Mahāyoga tantras such as the *Śrīparamādya*, invoke the state of great bliss (*mahāsukha*) through the elaborate conduct of the play of all the Tathāgatas— including the binding of the cross-legged posture, the nine dramatic sentiments (*nava-nāṭya-rasa*), and so forth; however, in this *Śrīguhyasamāja*, only the non-elaborate (*niṣprapañcatā*) and the utterly non-elaborate (*atyanta-niṣprapañcatā*) conduct are taught.

CMP09.054. Now, the elaborate practice (*prapañca-caryā*) is introduced from the *Śrī-sarvabuddhasamāyoga-ḍākinījālasaṃvara-mahāyogatantra*. CMP09.055. Now, therefore, I shall fully proclaim the supreme universal mandala, the *Sarvabuddhasamāyoga-ḍākinījālasaṃvara*. CMP09.056. [The *Sarvabuddhasamāyoga-ḍākinījālasaṃvara*]...
CMP09.057/ Always abiding in the supreme, most delightful secret, which is the self of all;
CMP09.058/ the glorious one, consisting of all Buddhas, the arising of Vajrasattva, is bliss;
CMP09.059/ adorned with the great divine net of jewels of the Tathāgatas, and so forth.
Then, in a residence adorned with bells, covered by a canopy, and radiant, or alternatively in gardens and such places,
they practice the *Sarvabuddhasamāyoga-ḍākinījālasaṃvara*.
CMP09.063. Having first placed a seat there that produces pleasure through its soft touch, CMP09.064. for that is indeed the seat of all Buddhas, covered by a cloth of universal lotuses. CMP09.065.
For it is there that the forms of the glorious Vajrasattva truly manifest their miraculous transformations.
CMP09.066/ It may consist of all the elements, or likewise be made of living wood;
CMP09.067/ it should be consecrated with its own presiding deity through the faces, signs, and mudrās. CMP09.068/ Whether it be cast, forged, consecrated, or beautifully painted,
CMP09.069/ One should fashion various reflected images and symbolic seals (mudrās). CMP09.070/ With faces representing one's own presiding deity, [one should visualize] a woman who is well-adorned.
CMP09.071/ One should fashion the Gaṇamaṇḍala as being auspicious with the symbols and seals of one's own mudrā.
CMP09.072. I shall explain the meaning of these sūtras in detail.

CMP09.073. First of all, in a secluded place such as a garden that is agreeable to the mind and free from unworthy persons such as śrāvakas and others, one should have constructed a temple of three stories made of brick, adorned with various artistic works;
therein, in the first story, one should establish a kitchen.
In the second city, one should place the ritual implements for worship, such as lutes and songs;
in the third city, may the illustrious Viśva, the most fortunate, sport together with the yoginīs.

Alternatively, having visualized within the underground chamber (bhūgṛha)—which is provided with strong walls and so forth, and consists of a ground made of various ornaments and vajras—a gabled temple (kūṭāgāra) on the peak of the Vajra-Meru mountain, composed of crystal, lapis lazuli, sapphire, emerald, and ruby.
CMP09.075. Quadrangular, with four doors, and adorned with four archways; CMP09.076. Equipped with four boundary lines, and beautified by eight pillars; CMP09.077.
Decorated with strings and half-strings of pearls, and embellished with cloth garlands and wreaths.
Adorned with the splendor of bells and banners, and decorated with chowries and the like;
with half-moons and vajras at the corners, and at the junctions of the doorways and turrets;
and embellished with various cloths such as the *pakṣiṇī* and the *kramaśīrṣa*.

CMP09.081. Therein, the practitioner, authorized by his gurus, having worshipped the great lords of yogins—both those who have attained realization and those who have not—together with their beloved companions, such as consorts and attendants, who have cast off ordinary egoism, should enter the practice of Mahāmudrā with a fearless mind like a lion, according to this sequence.
CMP09.082. In this regard, the sequence is as follows:
Having first taken ultimate truth as his object of focus, he brings himself to completion in the form of Vajrasattva through the process of self-consecration (svādhiṣṭhāna-krama).
Seated as the sovereign of the maṇḍala, he experiences the sense-object of form.

Then, in order to manifest the illusory forms of the consorts of all the Tathāgatas, a certain woman stands before the Blessed One in the form of Saṃvarī, her very nature being the continuity of passion.

One [goddess], in the form of *ah*, by virtue of having the nature of the continuum of sexual bliss (*surata-santati*), is situated in the southern direction; one, in the form of *pra*, by virtue of having the nature of the continuum of wrath (*raudra-santati*), is situated in the western direction;
and one, in the form of *śi*, by virtue of having the nature of the continuum of life-force (*jīva-santati*), is situated in the northern direction.
These are the female companions:
one, in the form of the awakening of a Buddha, is situated in the southeast corner for the purification of delusion;
another, in the form of the wheel of Dharma, is situated in the southwest corner for the purification of the pride that leaps across and overcomes the three worlds.

One, in the form of Trailokyavijayā, is stationed in the northwest corner for the removal of hatred; another, in the form of Kāmalatā, is stationed in the northeast corner for the removal of passion and darkness;
and another, in the form of Śuṣirā, is stationed in the outer southeast corner.

One, assuming the form of Nṛtyā and bringing the three worlds under her control by playing the vīṇā of love, is stationed in the outer south-west corner; one, assuming the form of Vitatā and removing poison and fever by playing the mukunda drum, is stationed in the outer north-west corner;
and one, assuming the form of Ghanā and [removing] ailments by playing the muraja drum, is stationed in the outer north-east corner.

One [deity], in the form of Vajrapuṣpā, with hands occupied by flowers, is stationed on the outer fillet in the southeast corner; one, in the form of Vajradhūpā, holding an incense burner, is stationed in the southwest corner;
and one, in the form of Vajrālokā, holding a great lamp, is stationed in the northwest corner.

One [deity], in the form of Vajragandhā, holding a conch filled with fragrance in her hand, is stationed in the northeast corner on the outer panel itself (CMP 09.086). One, in the form of a horse, born from the neighing of a supreme steed, dries up the three worlds and is stationed having performed the protection of the eastern gate. One, in the form of Vajramukhī, withdrawing the three realms, is stationed having performed the protection of the southern gate.
One, surveying the three worlds in the form of Vajrāloka, stands established as the guardian of the western gate;

another, in the form of Bhasmapralayavetālī, reviving even those reduced to ashes by providing consolation to the realms of Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Svaḥ, stands established as the guardian of the northern gate.

Therein, the Blessed One, the Universal Monarch of Great Bliss, having first recollected the meditative absorption whose nature is the reality of things (*bhūtatanaya*), generates a distinguished sense of self-identity, thinking, "I shall please all the Tathāgatas residing within the maṇḍala of my own body. First, he relishes the three kinds of sensory objects, such as form and so forth; thereafter, having prepared all food by means of the two-fold procedure beginning with purification, and having recollected the naturally perfected internal hearth, he generates the sense of self-identity, thinking, "I offer [this] as oblations into the mouth of the Samādhisattva, in the midst of the three-pointed fire," and thus consumes it.
Then, it is easily digested and becomes an elixir (*rasāyana*).
In this way, the practitioner, having satisfied the body-vajra with foods to be chewed, eaten, drunk, and so forth, finally experiences the fifth sense-object, touch.

Following this sequence, having seen the circle of goddesses such as Sahacarī and the others as being skilled in passion, he takes his chosen mudrā, places her on his lap, and generates a firm resolve, thinking: "I shall accomplish the siddhi of the Mahāmudrā. [He then engages in] embracing, kissing, and sucking.

Having performed the striking with the nails, the hissing sound, the cooing of the cuckoo, the humming of the bee, the stimulation of the channels, and so forth, and having assumed the postures such as the Tathāgata-paryaṅka, Vajra-paryaṅka, Ratna-paryaṅka, Padma-paryaṅka, and Karma-paryaṅka, one should remain established in the ritual action.

Then, through the arousal of the vajra-lotus and the meditative union (*samāpatti*) of wisdom and means, one causes all the Tathāgatas—the intrinsic nature of the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth—to descend from the crown of the head through the seventy-two thousand channels (*nāḍī*) in the form of a continuous stream. Having melted the vowels and consonants (*alikāli*), they fall according to the sequence of passion, dispassion, and intermediate passion, becoming the very embodiment of the Perfection of Wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) and personally realized within oneself.

Thus, having practiced the glorious samādhi of great bliss (*mahāsukha*) and attained its excellence, the yogi matures sentient beings right there in the maṇḍala of the assembly through both restraint and grace.

For certain individuals who hold the view of attachment to emptiness, that very Blessed One, in the form of Mahāvairocana, through the *mahāśāntika* samādhi, demonstrates the characteristic of non-abiding nirvāṇa—neither empty nor non-empty—and thereby suppresses their view of emptiness.
Likewise, for those who are extremely fierce and difficult to discipline, he suppresses their contemptible views through the wrathful samādhi of Śrī Vajraheruka and then bestows grace upon them.
For those with false views, he demonstrates the ultimate truth in the form of Padmanarteśvara and brings them under his control.

For those who are extremely base, miserly, and greedy, he suppresses their afflictions and wrong views by means of the great *pauṣṭika* (nourishing) samādhi in the form of the illustrious Vajrasūrya, raining down all wealth and jewels. For those whose vigor is extremely base, he suppresses their lack of vigor through valor, by means of the *haṭhayoga* samādhi in the form of a supreme steed.

CMP09.090. Therein, the Blessed One, the Glorious Mahāsukha, for the purpose of demonstrating the nature of the great play (*mahāralli-krīḍā*) of the Dharma-cloud (*dharmodaya*), and with a mind focused on nothing else for the sake of mutual exhilaration, performs the dance of the Buddhas (*buddha-nāṭya*) in this sequence: seal (*mudrā*) and counter-seal (*pratimudrā*), salutation (*vandana*) and counter-salutation (*prativandana*), worship (*pūjā*) and counter-worship (*pratipūjā*), drama (*nāṭaka*) and counter-drama (*pratināṭaka*), song (*gīta*) and counter-song (*pratigītaka*), physical gestures (*kāya-cchomā*), and vocal gestures (*vāk-cchomā*). Communication is carried out by means of these signs (*saṅketa*). CMP09.091. Therein, the vocal gesture (*vāk-cchomā*) is explained:
Oṃ ati hoḥ! One should indicate, "I bow to this barbarian. Oṃ prati! Again, for each prostration, [one says] "ccheṃ," which is the salutation to the Ācārya.
O Bhakṣa, enter;
O Cchvo, welcome; O Cchaṃ, you who encompass all.
Khaṃ! Eat!
Khaḥ! Devour! Draṃ draṃ! The flesh!
Śraṃ śraṃ [conveys] blood; dreṃ dreṃ [conveys] flesh; recite "prabhakṣa" [meaning] consume; [recite] "vajrodaka" [meaning] adamantine water.
Soma is the five nectars; wine is the drink for the night.
Saṃvara, Udaka,
Supriya, Puṣpa, Sañcaya, and Phala.
*Jālakaṃ* means cloth;
*kṣam* means a house; *kṣorṇṇam* means one's own home.
The wish-fulfilling deity-abode is the throwing mandala;
the awakener is the mandala master.
The disciple is the means;
the friend is the brother who has pleased the deity.
The Vajrayoginī is hidden;
her city is the Dākinī,
the Viklavā Mothers.
One's own father is like a mute; a worthy son is *prīṃ prīṃ* [to his father], and a daughter is *prīṃ*.
Abundance, material form, rolling about, sexual intercourse with those who should not be approached, and joy as food.
Give the substance of the bow;
go, go; come, come.
There is no wandering about, no anger,
and no casting off or killing.
The protection of living beings, detachment from worldly water, and the passion for modesty.
Having worshipped the liquid substance in due order while saying, "O you who are *surata*," one should perform the recollection of one's own deity while saying,
"I am *surata*."
"I am impassioned" is the response for the practice of Vajrasattva;
"I am awakened" is the response for the practice of Śrī-Vairocana.
"I rejoice" is the response of the practitioner of Herukavajra;
"I am filled with passion" is the response.
"I rejoice" is the response; this is the *sādhana* of Vajrasūrya. The *sādhana* of Śrī Padmanarteśvara is as follows: [B:63a]
"I shall rub [you]" is the reply;
"O means of the supreme horse," "those goddesses are to be honored," and "you are the pledge"— this indeed is the speech.
For the purpose of recollecting one’s own deity,
there is the utterance "I am Samaya," and [the mantra] "Obeisance to the worshipper of the assembly of the maṇḍala of the fortunate Śrī Vajrasattva."
The sequence for the turning of the verbal signs (*vāk-chomā*) has been concluded. Now, the bodily signs (*kāya-chomā*) are explained:
by touching the head, one performs a salutation.
From touching the forehead, there is a return salutation;
from the raising of the right eyebrow, success in one's undertaking;
and from the left, victory.
From the throbbing of the left eye, a woman becomes beautiful; from the right, a man becomes handsome.
From the touch of the left ear, one attains a happy state.
When well-spoken words are uttered on the right,
by touching the right nostril, it bestows incense; on the left, it bestows fragrance.
By licking the right side of the tongue, she offers meat; by the left, she offers wine;
and by touching the left side of the belly, she offers food.
"Offering a condiment with the right hand" is the sequence for the transformation of the bodily gestures (kāyacchomā).

Having thus cast aside worldly meditation and relinquished the sovereignty of the mind, always dwelling in a joyful state of mind and sporting with the yoginīs just like King Indrabhūti, he transforms his physical body into a vajra-body; then, together with his harem, he becomes invisible and travels from buddha-field to buddha-field, endowed with the eightfold sovereign powers.
As it is stated in the *Mūlatantra* (CMP 9.95–96):
"While enjoying all the offerings of the goddesses according to one's pleasure,
one should worship one's own self through the yoga of one's own presiding deity."
One should worship through moderate application all the pleasures of yoga (CMP09.097);
yet, by savoring them with excessive application, one attains accomplishment (CMP09.098).
Through this pleasure of the elixir, which is the very self of all Buddhas (CMP09.099), [one succeeds].
CMP09.100/ May there be success in long life, youth, health, and true happiness for Śrī Vajrasattva.
CMP09.101/ [He is] the great body of all Buddhas, the Sarasvatī of all Buddhas,
CMP09.102/ the great mind of all Buddhas, and the great festival of all Buddhas.
CMP09.103/ He is the great king of all Buddhas, the sovereign lord of all Vajra-holders;
CMP09.104/ the lord of all Lokeśvaras, the sovereign lord of all jewels.
CMP09.105/ Sporting with them, he proceeds toward birth for those who desire it.

CMP09.106: The universal sovereign, the great siddha of all goddesses, is accomplished. CMP09.107: Alternatively, for one who has little wealth and is unable to constantly carry out the extensive elaborations of play according to the sequence just described, "freedom from elaboration" (*niṣprapañcatā*) and "utter freedom from elaboration" (*atyanta-niṣprapañcatā*) are taught here in the *Śrī-saṃvara*.
Demonstrating that practice, he says:
"Every day, or every month, or likewise every year, or even according to one's specific empowerment, one should perform the ritual dance of the Buddha-saṃvara. (CMP 09.108–09.109)
Whether standing or sitting, walking or remaining as one is,
whether rejoicing or conversing, in whatever place and in whatever manner—
whatever [object] comes within the range of the senses, each of those [is to be understood] by its own nature.
CMP09.113: By means of the yoga of non-concentration, one should carry [the mind] as consisting of all Buddhas. CMP09.114:
Equal to space, having the nature of space, limitless, like the ocean.
CMP09.115: This is the teaching on the method of the dharma of passion; it is playfulness, an extensive sport.
CMP09.116/ And the mere object is grasped for the purpose of instructing the disciple. CMP09.117/ How many future births can be spoken of? Thus, the teaching on passion is permitted.

The Ninth Chapter: The Resolution of Doubts Concerning the Integration of the Elaborations of the Awakening to the Source of Phenomena (*dharmodayā*) through the Conduct of a Bodhisattva, according to the System of the *Śrī-sarvabuddhasamāyoga-ḍākinījālasaṃvara*.
Chapter Ten: The Resolution of Doubts Concerning the Integration of Non-elaborated Conduct (*niṣprapañcacaryā*). CMP10.001.
The Vajra-disciple said:
"The practice with conceptual elaboration has been clearly explained; may the Blessed One, the Vajra-teacher and Instructor, now point out the practice without conceptual elaboration.
The Vajra-teacher replied:

Excellent, excellent, O Mahāsattva! According to the tradition of the *Śrī-Guhyasamāja-Mahāyogatantra*, I shall set forth the practice free from conceptual proliferation; listen with a one-pointed mind.
This compendium of meditative concentration is to be accomplished in great forest regions adorned with fruits, flowers, and the like, or on a secluded mountain.
CMP10.005/ In a location favorable to the mind as described in the tantras and so forth, having consecrated an earthen cell or a palace according to the prescribed ritual,
and having constructed therein a gabled chamber (kūṭāgāra) with a pinnacle of vajras and jewels, endowed with qualities such as being square and so on,
the great yogin— having abandoned ordinary ego-grasping— and having also consecrated an external consort, [proceeds].
Together with a circle of disciples bound by a single birth, one should begin the practice of Mahāmudrā according to the sequence to be described.
In this regard, the sequence is as follows:

first, having relied upon ultimate truth, one emerges through the process of self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhāna-krama*) and, by entering into the emission of Akṣobhya, one is established as the sovereign of the maṇḍala.

Then, having removed the ordinary ego-sense, and having resolved that those whose retinues are indivisible have become constituent parts of the maṇḍala of one’s own body in the form of the deities of the maṇḍala such as Vairocana and the rest, and having caused the entire circle to be filled with passion, one enters ultimate truth through the sequence of grasping the mass together with one’s own mudrā and its subsequent dissolution.

Then, exhorted by the goddesses Locanā and the others through verses beginning with "O Vajracitta," which represent the purification of the four Brahma-abodes, you are suddenly awakened through the process of self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhāna*). For the sake of experiencing the flavor of supreme bliss (*paramānanda*), you sport with the nine dramatic sentiments (*nava-nāṭya-rasa*).
Thus, repeatedly entering the limit of reality (*bhūta-koṭi*) and repeatedly emerging from it, you savor the five qualities of desire (*pañca-kāma-guṇa*) which have the nature of the five Tathāgatas;
in such a way that the mind does not wither, you accomplish the *tathāgatāralli* (the dance-play of the Tathāgatas).
Therein, one experiences the threefold object of form, such as visible forms;
one experiences the threefold object of sound, such as song, stringed instruments, and percussion;
and one experiences the threefold object of odor, such as flowers, incense, and ointments.
One experiences the threefold range of tastes, such as pungent, bitter, astringent, sour, and salty (CMP 10.008).

Then, having taken one from among those women who are like kinswomen—such as a Caṇḍālī, a washerwoman, a garland-maker, an actress, a basket-weaver, a craftsmaid, or one with a physical disability—who is sixteen years old, of intact virginity, whose limbs are bent low by the weight of full breasts, and who has undertaken the observances;

Then the great yogin, whose nature is non-conceptual, in order to demonstrate that his own self is the intrinsic nature of all phenomena, consecrates the objects of consumption—which are despised by the world—through the sequence of purification and so forth. Having removed the perception of worldly signs and remaining in a secluded place, he partakes [of them].

Furthermore, for him there is no binding of mudrās, no mandala, no sacrificial pit, no shrine, no recitation of books, no bodily mortification, and he does not prostrate before images made of cloth, wood, or stone.

He does not call to mind the refuge of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, nor does he employ the calculation of lunar days, astrological configurations, moments, constellations, or auspicious times; all of this he accomplishes through his own internal power alone (CMP 10.010). If, however, he lacks the necessary conditions and is unable to accomplish the maṇḍala of gathering, [he should proceed as follows].

Then, by that practitioner—even though he consists of the great reality of the five secrets—the practice of non-conceptual conduct (*niṣprapañca-caryā*) should be cultivated according to this sequence.
This is the sequence:

in a certain [direction], in the eastern corner, there stands one in the form of Rūpavajrā, her delicate lotus-hands holding a mirror, gazing with gentle eyes, her full breasts densely covered by a profusion of necklaces of countless pearls, her garment slightly loosened to reveal half her rounded hips, for the sake of inspiring great bliss and passion.

Another, in the form of Śabdavajrā, with wide-open eyes gazing [forward], stands in the southern corner, skilled in proclaiming the teaching of the Dharma through passionate conduct and graceful, playful movements, and through the singing and playing of lutes accompanied by soft,
melodic chants.

One [consort], in the form of Gandhavajrā, gazes with a smiling eye; her lotus-like hands are joined by copper-colored webbing, which shines with the rays from her smooth and elevated nails. Holding a vessel made of jewels and other materials in a dancing posture, she stands in the western corner as a carrier of fragrance, perfuming the chambers of the ten directions with the scent of saffron, agallochum, musk, uragasāra sandalwood, and camphor contained within that vessel.
Another [consort], in the form of Rasavajrā, gazes with honeyed eyes; she holds various side-dishes placed in many vessels of jewels, gold, and silver.

In the northern corner, seated upon a vessel of divine food—a great nectar consisting of wholesome meals of mixed flavors and the finest delicacies—is a certain woman in the form of Sparśavajrā. Her limbs are adorned with all the auspicious marks; she is beautiful with waves and ripples of the three folds [of skin] across her waist, while her middle is exceedingly slender. Her deep navel region possesses broad, clockwise-rotating whorls hidden by a line of hair, and her hips are thick and heavy.

With her gait, smile, and face rendered graceful and tender by a steady, amorous charm, she looked serene with a gentle gaze; established upon his lap due to her passion for great bliss (*mahāsukha*),
she was moved by the joy of the illustrious practice of the passion of sexual delight (*surata-sukha-rāga-carita*)—

through embracing, kissing, sucking, grasping the breasts, horripilation, striking, biting, scratching, drumming, swinging, piercing, and the movements of the elbows and so forth— her pearl necklace trembling.
Through the union of the vajra and lotus— the objects of the senses and the sounds of bracelets, armlets, earrings, and anklets—

and through the meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) of wisdom (*prajñā*) and means (*upāya*), the knowledge (*jñāna*) and the knowable (*jñeya*), by the churning of the vowels (*āli*) and consonants (*kāli*), the *madanātapatra*, the *kūrmakaṇṭha*, the moon, and the movement and impelling of the three channels (*nāḍī*) with the three fingers, all the Tathāgatas, whose nature is the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth, become liquefied in the form of a continuous stream of waterfalls; having reached the ground of gnosis (*jñānabhūmi*), one savors the state of supreme great bliss (*paramamahāsukhapada*).
Illuminating this point, the *Mūlatantra* (CMP 10.014) says:
"One who desires knowledge should always enjoy the five qualities of desire," even if the Rūpavajrās and others are not present.
Then, one should also accomplish [the practice] through the yoga of union with each individual Sparśavajrā,
because all the Tathāgatas are contained within the body-maṇḍala of the practitioner,
and all the goddesses are contained within the body-maṇḍala of Sparśavajrā.
Therefore, demonstrating in the Root Sūtra that one should practice with non-conceptualization and without differentiated ego-grasping, it says:

CMP 10.016: Then Vajrapāṇi, the Lord of all Tathāgatas, emitted from his own body, speech, and mind-vajras the conduct for undertaking the vows of the vidyā of the body, speech, and mind-vajras of all Tathāgatas.

CMP10.017/ One should perform the meditation on the body, speech, and mind as the vajras of body, speech, and mind; CMP10.018/ by means of their very own forms, that task is accomplished and accomplishment is swiftly attained.
CMP10.019/ In this regard, there is this vow of the vidyā of body, speech, and mind.

CMP10.020/ One should have a great image made, resembling white in color, wearing matted locks and a crown, according to the ritual rules of the entire commitment of the mantra-vow (mantra-saṃvara). CMP10.021-022/ Having taken a sixteen-year-old girl adorned with all ornaments...
Having obtained a woman with a beautiful face and large eyes, one should practice the vow of knowledge (vidyā-vrata).
One should meditate upon her through the enjoyment of her eyes and feet, which bear the marks of the vajra.
She should be one who knows the ritual procedures of mudrās and mantras, and is well-trained in the mantras and tantras.

In this way, one shall quickly become a Buddha, a Lord who is an ocean of great wisdom;
within just six months, one shall attain all of that—of this there is no doubt.
The practitioner, firm in resolve, should constantly wander for alms in the forest.
Terrified by fear, they offer them food adorned with divine [substances].
If one who is of the nature of a vajra should transgress [this], the indestructible vajra would be destroyed.
[This applies even to] a goddess, a nāginī, a great yakṣiṇī, an asurī, or even a human woman.
CMP 10.035: "Having attained the vow of knowledge (*vidyā-vrata*), one should practice the wisdom of the three vajras.
CMP 10.036: Thus, those belonging to the six desire realms experience the bliss of supreme joy moment by moment through sexual union consisting of embracing, holding hands, laughing, and gazing;
and in the state of perfection (*pariniṣpannāvasthā*), they become embodiments of constant bliss for as long as saṃsāra endures.
Illuminating this point, he says in the *Sarvadevasamāgama-tantra* (CMP 10.37–38):
"Through the union of the two organs, the method of exertion occurs internally;

The Tenth Chapter, titled "The Integration of Practice Free from Conceptual Elaboration and the Resolution of Doubts.
Chapter XI: The Chapter on the Integration of Practice that is Utterly Free from Conceptual Elaboration and the Resolution of Doubts.
CMP11.001/ Now, the practice that is utterly free from conceptual proliferation is introduced:
CMP11.002/ On secluded mountains and by river cascades,
CMP11.003/ and even in cremation grounds and similar places, this compendium of meditations should be practiced.
CMP11.004: In places such as those described in the tantras that are favorable to the mind, one should accomplish the Yakṣiṇīs, Kiṅkaras, and so forth for the sake of alms-bowls (*sarāva*).

Alternatively, having obtained mere food from a superior practitioner (*uttarasādhaka*) or at a great sacrificial feast (*mahāsattra*), one should enter the practice of absolute non-elaboration (*atyantanisprapañcacaryā*) by means of this sequence.
CMP11.005: In this regard, the sequence is as follows:
First, the practitioner, recollecting the experience of suffering throughout beginningless saṃsāra and desiring the bliss of nirvāṇa, must become one who has renounced all attachments;
even toward the sovereignty of a king, he must perceive it as suffering. Second, he should abandon the notion of possession regarding objects even as small as a sesame seed.
With reference to the third, the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), one should be indifferent toward body and life,
as it is said in the *Samādhirāja-sūtra* (CMP 11.006):
"Therefore, O youth, a bodhisattva who desires this samādhi and wishes to quickly awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment must be one who is not attached to body or life."

CMP11.007: Likewise, neither mundane minor accomplishments (*laukika-kṣudra-siddhi*) nor supramundane eight great accomplishments (*lokottara-aṣṭa-mahāsiddhi*) should be sought, because they involve distraction and lead to regression, as stated in the *Asādhāraṇa-guhya-mahāyoga-tantra*. CMP11.008:
Furthermore, for the sake of attaining the accomplishment of omniscience, one does not desire any other accomplishment whatsoever.

One should not pray for the accomplishment of all worldly bases and speech, the accomplishment of servants, the accomplishment of the auspicious vase, the accomplishment of the underworld, the accomplishment of sovereignty, the accomplishment of subjugation, the accomplishment of nourishment, or the accomplishment of malevolent rites.
Why is that?
Because one who seeks the great accomplishment does not desire a minor accomplishment.
One attains absorption solely in the accomplishment of the non-conceptual;
and so it is said in the *Guhyasiddhi*:
"The knower of reality should always avoid [ritual] applications and the like in their true nature."

CMP11.011/ Having abandoned the ego-identification with Vajrasattva, one should not perform [the practice] elsewhere. CMP11.012/ Even the application [of the practice] is not to be understood [as separate], for one is established in pure reality. CMP11.013/ This continues as long as one contemplates by means of the yoga of the state of selflessness.
For one who abides in the state of the absence of intrinsic nature and is endowed with divine means,
whatever is prescribed in the ritual manuals is accomplished through non-discursive [meditation];
by the power of the yoga of cultivation, it manifests of its own accord.
CMP11.017/ All of that, whatever constitutes the characteristics of accomplishment (*siddhi*), occurs in a mere instant.

CMP11.018/ Therefore, having set aside an external consort, one should adopt a bold resolve, thinking, "By means of union with the wisdom-seal (*jñānamudrā*) residing within the heart, I shall very swiftly accomplish the state of Mahāvajradhara," and meditate alone according to the sequence to be described.
CMP11.019/ In this regard, the sequence is as follows:

As long as the basket of the aggregates exists, the nature of the three types of consciousness—the self-nature and the other-nature of the manifestation of primordial matter—exists directly in the world.
How then could the first manifestation be the second nature? That [nature], conjoined with the wind, causes one to wander through the ten directions.
By what means? Through passion, dispassion, moderate passion, and so forth;

furthermore, through the fierce, the gentle, exhilaration, sorrow, hunger, thirst, pain, and so on. Having brought these one hundred and sixty types of dispositions (*prakṛti*) to mind day and night, they are obstructed within ignorance (*avidyā*), yet rising up again, they wander by the force of the wind;
therefore, there is agitation of the body.

As long as the sense faculties, beginning with the eye, do not perceive an object, they remain focused upon that very [object]. Due to habituation since beginningless time, one attains a refined application through the practice of the dharma of selflessness throughout the succession of births; having thus brought about the convergence of the appearances of intrinsic nature into a single point, one should take ultimate reality as the object of focus. By this sequence, CMP 11.020: therein, this is the sequence.
The aggregates and so forth enter into the subtle element;
the subtle element, in turn, enters into the mind; and the mind, again, enters into the mental factors.
Furthermore, when the mental factors (*caitasika*) are thus engaged with ignorance (*avidyā*), at that time one sleeps;

there is forgetfulness characterized by the entry of the mind, mental factors, and ignorance. Later, even that forgetfulness no longer exists, as it is released again by the wind, which moves according to its nature, [realizing] that the luminous (*prabhāsvara*) has the nature of gnosis (*jñāna*).
If there is no arising of another dream, as long as consciousness does not stir, one sleeps; one perceives that very luminosity,
which is to be personally realized, devoid of body, speech, and mind, the ultimate truth— this is called "inner awakening."
CMP11.021: By this sequence, one should cause the array of Tathāgatas residing in the body-maṇḍala to enter into suchness (*tathatā*); thus one will attain supreme accomplishment.

The meaning is that, regardless of the practices involving conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) or the absence of proliferation (*niṣprapañca*), here the transformation of one's own nature occurs even more swiftly. This very point is stated in the *Sandhyāvyākaraṇa-mahāyogatantra*:
CMP11.022: One should perceive internal phenomena such as form and so forth; this is called insight (vipaśyanā). CMP11.023:
One should conceptually arrange them according to their respective order, beginning with Akṣobhya and the others; this becomes calm abiding (śamatha). CMP11.024:
Because these two lack intrinsic nature, they are designated as "suchness" and "peace."
CMP11.025: "In the maṇḍala of suchness (tathatā), the yogin should cause all the Buddhas to enter.
CMP11.026: Furthermore, it is said in the *Sarvadevasamāgama-tantra*:
CMP11.027: "In the great, terrible fire of nirvāṇa, one is not released even as ashes."
CMP11.028/ Therefore, neither sense-object nor elements exist there.

CMP11.029/ Having ascertained the Mother of all Buddhas, who consists of realization, through this sequence by means of both reasoning and scripture, and having abandoned all conceptual proliferation and attachment to sense-objects,
one should practice the *bhusuku* conduct according to this order.
In this regard, the sequence is as follows:
having eaten with the thought "bhu," one pursues that alone and removes attachment by means of difficult observances.

Thinking "nothing at all should be thought," one should directly realize this cognition characterized by ignorance; that very cognition, marked by the form of the hook of ignorance, does not cause one to return again, but rather directly realizes the luminosity itself, which is stainless by nature.
Thinking "ku," one should go to a hut (*kuṭi*) for the purpose of voiding excrement and urine; one experiences only that.
One should remove attachment to the body, sensations, objects, and faculties, and one should not contemplate their intrinsic nature (CMP 11.031).
Even while practicing the conduct that is utterly free from conceptual proliferation through the vow of a madman, one should act according to the sequence taught in the explanatory tantras;
therein, this is the sequence:

CMP11.032–034: When the hero is free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpa*), having shattered worldly stability, he may perform all activities; at that time, the Buddhas behold him. Moving with skillful means like a child, he attains all accomplishments—of this there is no doubt.
CMP11.035. When the yogi is free from mental effort (*nirābhoga*), then all perfections rain down.
CMP11.036. For those possessed of every kind of evil, who are firmly established in the veil of delusion (*moha-āvaraṇa*), CMP11.037.
through the yoga of the madman’s vow (*unmatta-vrata*), unfailing success is achieved within six months.
CMP11.038: One shall personally behold all the Buddhas and be worshipped with all desired things.
CMP11.039: There is neither exhaustion nor decline; one’s body arises according to one's own wish for its lifespan.
CMP11.040: One attains supreme, ultimate enlightenment without effort.

CMP11.041/ Those who are eager for the happiness of all desires succeed without effort. CMP11.042/ Whether walking, standing, or sitting, one who constantly proceeds toward the supremely profound state—
CMP11.043/ This skill in luminous gnosis is the constant characteristic of yogins.
CMP11.044/ By means of this yoga of meditative concentration, the jewel of the mind becomes firm.
CMP11.045/ And the Buddhas, established in enlightenment, bestow their empowerment.
CMP11.046/ Having become thus and being firmly settled, one who is devoted to that state should cultivate it.
CMP11.047–049: As long as the mind is not weary, the wise one with a concentrated mind should remain thus;
but once weary, he may afterwards wander about, acting according to his inclination, while meditating on vast enlightenment with eyes slightly opened.
CMP 11.050: Sometimes laughing and sometimes speaking, he may remain stationary or engage in activity.

CMP 11.051: But with a mind intent on meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), so that no weariness arises, CMP 11.052: such is the case for the mantra-practitioner who is absorbed in *samādhi* and free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpa*).
CMP 11.053: "The unsurpassed state is accomplished by transcending the limitation of time.

CMP 11.054: Thus, through the distinctions of weak, medium, and intense, and according to what is appropriate, for one who practices the three types of conduct for a fortnight, a month, or up to six months, the signs of the accomplishment of Mahāmudrā arise; therein, these are the signs.
CMP11.055: Subtle form, light touch, and indeed pervasiveness;
CMP11.056: Radiance, stability, mastery, and the power to reach the end of desires.
CMP11.057: Furthermore, the signs of dream are stated in the *Śrī-Guhyasamāja-Mahāyoga-tantra*.
CMP11.058/ One sees the Buddha of radiant splendor, who has attained the pinnacle of the wisdom of awakening;
CMP11.059/ And one quickly perceives oneself as the Buddha’s sambhogakāya; CMP11.060/ And one sees oneself being honored by the great beings of the three realms.

He constantly beholds the great image of Vajrasattva, of supreme renown as Vajradharma, which is the source of the highest great gnosis, and is eternally worshipped by Buddhas and Bodhisattvas with the five strands of sensual pleasure.
The one of great renown, the Secret Vajra, beholds his own form in a dream;
the Great Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Vajra-holders pay him homage.
He shall see such dreams as bestow the accomplishments of body, speech, and mind.
Seeing a beautiful celestial maiden fully adorned with all ornaments,
or seeing a boy or a girl, he attains accomplishment;
he certainly beholds all the Buddhas residing in the fields of the ten directions.
With a joyful mind and self, one gives the delightful treasury of Dharma;
at the time of yoga, one sees all that which resides in the Dharma-body, surrounded by all sentient beings, established in the meditation-vajra.
CMP11.073: The Vajra-disciple said:

"If a practitioner, even though he has seen the truth, due to the force of the habituation of former latent tendencies (*vāsanā*), becomes distracted by activities such as agriculture, commerce, and service, and thus does not practice the threefold conduct; and because of the deficiency of necessary materials, he is unable to accomplish the ritual procedures exactly as taught in the Tantra—will he, upon passing away, attain rebirth in another life, or will he attain the state of a Mahāvajradhara?
CMP11.074: The Vajra-teacher replied:
CMP11.075: "Nothing is to be removed from this, nor is anything at all to be added. CMP11.076:
Reality is to be seen as it truly is; one who sees reality is liberated. CMP11.077:
This, namely, the vision of reality, is the designation for the perfected stage (*niṣpannakrama*).
Through the vision of reality (*bhūtadarśana*), views such as eternalism, nihilism, and transmigration are ceased;
nevertheless, relying upon conventional usage (*vyavahāra*), [there is] the purification of transmigration. *Glossaries* (end of MS B)
